cards.title: P versus NP
cards.formal: Does every language with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates admit a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm? Equivalently, do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and constants C,k such that, for every encoded Boolean formula F of bit length n, A decides whether F has a satisfying assignment and halts within $C(n+1)^k$ steps? The algorithm must give the correct answer on every input.
cards.definitions: A language is a subset of the finite binary strings. P consists of languages decided by one deterministic multitape Turing machine with worst-case running time C(n+1)^k for some constants C,k. NP consists of languages L for which there are a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p satisfying $x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|x|)}:V(x,y)=1$. The verifier's time is polynomial in the combined input length. SAT is the language of well-formed Boolean formulas with at least one satisfying assignment; malformed encodings are rejected. Fix any ordinary explicit binary encoding of formulas using AND, OR, and NOT. The question concerns uniform deterministic computation, with no advice, oracle, or error probability. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove P=NP or P≠NP in the deterministic uniform model defined here. Equality requires that every NP language have a polynomial-time decision algorithm; inequality requires that at least one NP language have none.
cards.why: This is the basic test of whether efficient verification entails efficient solution. It organizes the complexity of optimization, search, logical reasoning, and many graph problems, while motivating the development of general algorithmic lower-bound techniques.

importance.reason: The central boundary between efficient verification and efficient computation, with implications throughout TCS. It is the highest-priority landmark in the complexity category.

progress.text: The Cook–Levin completeness theorem identifies Boolean satisfiability as NP-complete; Karp reductions connect it to many standard combinatorial problems. This establishes equivalent targets, rather than a separation.

Relativization and subsequent natural-proofs and algebrization barriers delimit broad approaches to separation. The natural-proofs obstruction to general circuit lower bounds is conditional on sufficiently strong pseudorandomness assumptions.

Williams proves that NEXP is not contained in polynomial-size nonuniform ACC circuits, using faster satisfiability algorithms to obtain lower bounds. ACC has constant depth and modular counting gates. Both the larger language class and the restricted circuit model matter; this does not prove P≠NP.
The Clay Mathematics Institute continues to list P versus NP among its unsolved Millennium Prize Problems.

context_blocks.text: A proposed assignment to a Boolean formula is easy to check: evaluate the formula under that assignment. Finding a satisfying assignment seems to demand a different kind of work because the assignment is missing. The question asks whether this difference can always be overcome with only polynomial computation. It is a worst-case statement about arbitrarily long inputs, so extensive experiments on current SAT solvers cannot settle it.

NP-completeness makes SAT a representative of an entire class. A polynomial-time reduction converts any NP verification problem into a satisfiability instance while preserving its answer. Consequently, one polynomial-time SAT algorithm would supply polynomial-time decision procedures for all NP languages. It would also allow witnesses to be recovered by asking a sequence of decision questions about their successive bits.

The two possible answers have different practical limits. P=NP would not by itself give a small polynomial exponent or an implementation useful at realistic sizes. P≠NP would establish some worst-case superpolynomial difficulty, but would not imply an exponential lower bound, hardness of typical instances, or the existence of secure cryptography. Those are stronger or differently quantified claims.

Many successful lower bounds impose restrictions on the competing computations, such as bounded circuit depth or the absence of negation. Removing those restrictions is a central obstacle. Conversely, theorems about relativization, natural proofs, and algebrization identify limitations of particular proof methods. These results do not decide P versus NP.

cards.title: NP versus P/poly
cards.formal: Is $\mathrm{NP}\nsubseteq\mathrm{P/poly}$? Precisely, does there exist one language L∈NP such that, for every integer k≥1, real C>0, and integer N≥1, some n≥N satisfies $\operatorname{CC}(L_n)>C(n+1)^k$, where Lₙ is the characteristic function of L on n-bit inputs and CC is minimum Boolean circuit size?
cards.definitions: A Boolean circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with n input bits, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, constants 0 and 1, and one output bit. There are no depth or fan-out restrictions; a gate output may be reused arbitrarily. Size counts AND, OR, and NOT gates. Lₙ must be computed exactly on every n-bit string. A family {Cₙ} is nonuniform: no algorithm is required to construct Cₙ from n, and the circuit may depend arbitrarily on the input length, but not on the particular input of that length. P/poly consists of languages having circuits of size at most C(n+1)^k for some fixed constants C,k and every n. NP consists of languages L with a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and polynomial p such that x∈L iff some y of length at most p(|x|) satisfies V(x,y)=1. The existentially chosen language L is the same for every exponent k. The lower bound need only hold at arbitrarily large lengths for each k; an eventual bound at every sufficiently large length would be stronger. Equivalently, ask whether the NP-complete language SAT has no polynomial-size circuit family under an ordinary explicit binary formula encoding.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove NP is not contained in P/poly, or prove the containment. A positive separation requires one NP language escaping every polynomial circuit-size bound. Proving that, for each exponent k, a possibly different language requires more than n^k gates does not suffice. Containment can be established by giving polynomial-size circuits for SAT at every input length; an efficient uniform circuit generator is not required.
cards.why: This is the main unrestricted Boolean circuit lower-bound conjecture for efficiently verifiable problems. Circuits remove issues of uniform program construction and expose a finite combinatorial object, making the problem a central route toward unconditional computational lower bounds. It connects complexity classes, pseudorandomness, learning, and limitations of proof techniques.

importance.reason: A foundational strengthening of P≠NP and the central target of general Boolean circuit lower bounds. Its consequences and methods reach across complexity, derandomization, learning, and cryptography.

progress.text: The Karp–Lipton theorem shows NP⊆P/poly implies PH=Σ₂^P. Wigderson’s Theorem 5.5 records this consequence next to Conjecture 5.4.

Chen, Tal, and Wang obtain n^(2.5−ε) gate lower bounds against depth-two linear-threshold circuits for a function in E^NP, for every ε>0. Their introduction identifies NP⊄P/poly as the flagship open target.

context_blocks.text: A polynomial-time algorithm yields a polynomial-size circuit for each input length by unrolling its computation. The converse fails because a different circuit may be selected for every length without any effective way to generate those circuits. The conjecture asks whether NP retains hard problems even after granting this substantial extra freedom. A separation would imply P≠NP, while P≠NP alone does not establish the circuit claim.

Counting arguments show that most truth tables need exponentially many gates. They do not produce the required language in NP: an arbitrary sequence of hard truth tables need not have efficiently verifiable membership certificates. This is the central explicitness difficulty. It is also why enumerating hard functions at a few fixed lengths cannot satisfy the quantified statement on this card.

The Karp–Lipton theorem gives a consequence of the opposite outcome: if NP has polynomial-size circuits, the polynomial hierarchy collapses to its second level. This is evidence linking nonuniform algorithms to uniform complexity, but it is not a contradiction because the hierarchy is not known to be infinite.

The natural-proofs theorem identifies a conditional obstacle to a broad family of circuit lower-bound techniques. Under sufficiently strong pseudorandom-function assumptions, a property of truth tables that is both efficiently recognizable and sufficiently common cannot distinguish all hard functions from polynomial-size circuits in the required way. The theorem constrains a method, not every possible proof.

Williams’ separation for nondeterministic exponential time and constant-depth modular circuits demonstrates that faster satisfiability algorithms can yield nonuniform lower bounds. It leaves two restrictions relative to this target: the hard language may lie above NP, and the competing circuits have constant depth.

cards.title: NP versus coNP
cards.formal: Do there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a fixed polynomial p such that, for every Boolean CNF formula F, $F\text{ is unsatisfiable}\iff\exists\pi\in\{0,1\}^{\le p(|F|)}:V(F,\pi)=1$, with V never accepting a certificate for a satisfiable formula? Equivalently, is NP=coNP? The verification algorithm and polynomial are fixed for all formulas.
cards.definitions: A CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of literals x or NOT x. Variables take values in {0,1}; unsatisfiable means that no assignment makes all clauses true. The formula is encoded explicitly in binary, and |F| is its total bit length, including variable names and all literal occurrences. Empty clauses and an empty conjunction have their usual false and true meanings. V halts in time polynomial in |F|+|pi| on every pair of strings and rejects malformed formula encodings. Certificates may be arbitrary binary strings; they are not restricted to any particular inference calculus. NP is the class of languages with polynomial-length certificates checked in deterministic polynomial time. coNP consists of complements of NP languages. No randomization, oracle, advice, or interaction with a prover is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a sound verifier and one polynomial length bound covering every unsatisfiable formula, or prove that no such verifier and bound exist. Equivalently, prove NP=coNP or NP≠coNP. A lower bound for a particular proof system is insufficient for separation, and an efficient algorithm for finding certificates is not required for equality.
cards.why: This asks whether every nonexistence claim with an efficiently verifiable positive counterpart also has concise evidence. It is a central bridge between computational complexity, the length of mathematical proofs, and the limits of automated reasoning.

importance.reason: A fundamental certificate-complexity question that implies P≠NP in the separation direction and motivates the entire general proof-complexity lower-bound program.

progress.text: Cook and Reckhow establish the equivalence between NP=coNP and the existence of a polynomially bounded propositional proof system. This turns a complexity-class question into a precise proof-length target.

Haken proves an exponential resolution lower bound for pigeonhole formulas; Buss gives polynomial-size Frege proofs of the pigeonhole principle. These results demonstrate why lower bounds must account for the chosen proof system.

The ICTS program Circuits, Communication, and Proofs continues to present separation of NP from coNP as the goal of the Cook–Reckhow program. It describes current connections with circuit lower bounds and communication complexity; it announces no resolution of this question.

cards.status_note: The unrestricted certificate question remains a research target in the August 2026 primary workshop description. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate a resolution. Lower bounds for individual proof systems do not establish the universal separation.

context_blocks.text: A satisfiable formula has a direct certificate: a satisfying assignment. For an unsatisfiable formula, one must explain why every possible assignment fails. Listing all assignments and a violated clause for each gives a checkable certificate, but its length can be exponential. The question asks whether some fixed verification scheme can always compress this explanation to polynomial length.

Simple contradictions already have short certificates. For instance, the conjunction of the one-literal clauses x and NOT x has no satisfying assignment, which can be checked immediately. The difficulty is a universal guarantee over all formulas, including large contradictions whose structure does not reveal such a local conflict. The verifier must be sound even on adversarially chosen purported proofs.

Cook and Reckhow formalized proof systems by requiring efficient verification, soundness, and completeness. Their connection with complexity theory says that a polynomially bounded propositional proof system exists exactly when NP=coNP. The theorem permits any efficiently checked proof format. Restricting the allowed inference rules changes the problem to one about the power of that particular system.

This also distinguishes the question from P versus NP. If NP differs from coNP, then P differs from NP because deterministic polynomial time is closed under complement. The converse implication is not known. Equal certificate classes would still leave open whether those certificates can be found efficiently. Thus the target is symmetry between short evidence for yes and no answers, rather than an algorithm for deciding every NP problem.

Restricted lower bounds are nevertheless instructive. The pigeonhole principle has exponentially long resolution refutations in its usual encoding, while stronger Frege reasoning has polynomial-size proofs of the same principle. A formula family hard for one proof language therefore need not be hard for another.

cards.title: Superlinear Boolean circuit lower bounds
cards.formal: Does there exist a total function F:{0,1}*→{0,1}*, computable by one deterministic polynomial-time algorithm and satisfying |F(x)|=|x|, such that its unrestricted Boolean circuit complexity is not O(n)? Explicitly, for every C>0 and N≥1, must some n≥N satisfy CC(Fₙ)>Cn?
cards.definitions: Fₙ is the restriction of F to n-bit inputs, with n output bits. CC(Fₙ) is the least number of gates in a directed acyclic Boolean circuit computing all these outputs exactly on every input. Each gate may compute any Boolean function of at most two input bits: the full B₂ basis, including AND, OR, XOR and negation. Input nodes, constants 0 and 1, and designated output wires are free; gates have unrestricted fan-out and there is no depth bound. Gates may be shared among outputs. The family of competing circuits is nonuniform: the circuit at one input length need have no effective relationship to circuits at other lengths. In contrast, explicitness of F means a single deterministic Turing machine outputs F(x) in at most p(|x|) steps for one fixed polynomial p, with no advice. The empty input has empty output. This card fixes a polynomial-time interpretation of the source’s broader word “explicit” and preserves its allowance of n output bits. Changing between B₂ and the usual bounded-fan-in AND/OR/NOT basis changes size by at most a constant factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Exhibit one such polynomial-time function and prove that CC(Fₙ)/n is unbounded along arbitrarily large input lengths, or prove that every polynomial-time length-preserving function has O(n)-size nonuniform circuits, with the hidden constant allowed to depend on the function. A fixed bound such as 10n is insufficient. The precise target is not O(n); it does not additionally require the ratio to tend to infinity at every sufficiently large length. A superlinear single-output example would also settle the question after padding the output with zeros.
cards.why: This asks for the first unbounded improvement over linear size for an efficiently computable unrestricted circuit task. It isolates a basic gap between knowing that hard functions abound and proving hardness for one explicitly computable function.

importance.reason: A fundamental lower-bound milestone for unrestricted computation, with connections to matrix complexity, proof techniques and the limitations of nonuniform algorithms.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No superlinear unrestricted Boolean circuit lower bound for a polynomial-time length-preserving function was located. The question fixes the source’s explicitness convention; recent gate-simplification, covering and conditional natural-proofs results do not furnish such an example.

context_blocks.text: A circuit is a finite computation with a separate design for each input length. Intermediate results can be used many times, and different output bits can share the same work. This sharing is a central source of power: a lower bound for formulas, which cannot freely reuse intermediate results, need not hold for circuits. The target here leaves depth, fan-out and Boolean operations unrestricted apart from the two-input gate bound.

The explicitness requirement prevents a counting argument from solving the problem. There are vastly more Boolean functions than small circuits, so most functions require exponentially many gates. But describing one by its entire truth table takes exponential space, and selecting the first hard truth table by exhaustive search need not yield a polynomial-time function. We need an efficiently specified computation and a proof that every circuit for it exceeds every fixed linear bound.

Multi-output functions make the question especially concrete. A fixed, efficiently constructible binary matrix Aₙ defines Fₙ(x)=Aₙx over the two-element field. Its n outputs are parity sums of selected inputs. Computing every output separately can cost Θ(n²), yet a clever circuit may share partial sums across rows. Counting proves that some matrices need Ω(n²/log n) gates, but an explicit superlinear lower bound remains unknown even for this linear-algebra setting. A lower bound against XOR-only circuits would not automatically rule out smaller circuits that use nonlinear Boolean gates.

The polynomial-time convention also separates this question from NP versus P/poly. The desired F already has polynomial-size circuits because its algorithm can be simulated by circuits. Showing that it lacks linear-size circuits would separate two size scales within efficient nonuniform computation; it would not establish P≠NP. Conversely, proving superpolynomial circuit lower bounds for an NP language would address a stronger resource barrier but would not by itself make that language a polynomial-time example for this card.

cards.title: L versus NL
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine A and an absolute constant C such that, for every directed graph G on vertices {1,...,n} and every s,t, A decides whether t is reachable from s while using at most $C\log_2(n+2)$ work-tape cells? G is supplied explicitly as a read-only adjacency matrix, together with s and t. The machine must halt and be correct on every input. This is equivalent to L=NL.
cards.definitions: The graph may have self-loops; reachability allows a path of length zero, so s=t is a yes instance. Input access is two-way and read-only. Work tapes have a fixed finite alphabet; visited work-tape cells, including all counters and stored vertex identifiers, count toward space. The finite control and read-only input cells do not. There is no advice, random tape, oracle, writable copy of the input, or external storage. L is deterministic O(log N) work space on binary inputs of bit length N. NL uses the same space bound with nondeterministic transitions and accepts exactly when some computation branch accepts; all branches can be clocked to halt within polynomial time. Since the matrix encoding has N=Theta(n^2) bits, O(log N)=O(log n). A halting deterministic machine with this space bound automatically runs in polynomial time: it cannot repeat a complete configuration.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an always-correct deterministic logarithmic-space reachability algorithm for all directed graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. By NL-completeness under deterministic logspace reductions, either direction settles L versus NL. An algorithm for undirected graphs, a nondeterministic algorithm, or an algorithm using a larger power of log n does not answer the stated question.
cards.why: Directed reachability is the canonical model of exploring possible computational states. Its space complexity determines whether nondeterministic logarithmic memory can be replaced by deterministic logarithmic memory, with consequences for low-memory graph algorithms and complexity theory.

importance.reason: A central space-complexity separation expressed by a basic graph problem. The contrast with solved undirected reachability isolates a fundamental role of edge direction and nondeterminism.

progress.text: Savitch proves that nondeterministic space s can be simulated deterministically in O(s²) space, for s at least logarithmic. Directed reachability consequently has an O(log² n)-space algorithm.

Immerman and Szelepcsényi independently establish closure of nondeterministic space under complementation. In particular NL=coNL, so both reachability and nonreachability admit nondeterministic logspace algorithms.
Reingold obtains deterministic logarithmic space for undirected connectivity, published at STOC 2005 and subsequently in JACM. Arbitrary directed graphs are outside that theorem.

Doron, Pyne, Tell, and Williams give two algorithms such that, on each directed graph, at least one succeeds: deterministic polynomial-time, polylogarithmic-space transitive closure, or nondeterministic logarithmic-space random-walk estimation. This per-graph alternative does not give the first algorithm on every graph or reduce its space to O(log n).

Bhadra and Tewari show NL-hardness even for directed graphs whose edges can be partitioned into two forests of directed paths of length at most two, including when the partition is supplied. Such a simple decomposition therefore does not make the general logspace obstacle disappear.

context_blocks.text: A graph search usually remembers which vertices it has visited. With only logarithmic space, it can store a constant number of vertex names and counters, but cannot keep a separate visited bit for every vertex. The input may be rescanned as often as necessary. The challenge is to organize those repeated scans so that arbitrary directed paths can be detected without retaining a large search frontier.

Nondeterminism gives a simple logarithmic-space procedure: keep the current vertex and a length counter, guess the next edge, and accept if t is reached within n−1 edges. Any reachable target has a simple path within that bound. For a general nondeterministic logspace computation, vertices can instead represent machine configurations. An accepting computation becomes a directed path, explaining why this graph problem captures the whole class NL.

Savitch’s algorithm recursively asks whether a path can pass through a candidate midpoint. It saves space by recomputing subproblems, but a logarithmic recursion depth with logarithmic information per level uses O(log² n) space. Its running time is quasipolynomial. Reducing the storage to a single logarithmic factor would also force polynomial time in the stated machine model.

For undirected graphs, Reingold already achieved the logarithmic target. Edge direction is therefore a substantive part of this card. Likewise, NL=coNL shows that nonreachability has a nondeterministic logspace procedure; it does not remove nondeterminism. Recent connections with random-walk estimation make the landscape richer, while leaving the same deterministic directed question.

cards.definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All n² index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of b=d⌈log₂(n+2)⌉ bits for some fixed integer d≥3 chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2ᵇ, quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by O(n log n) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the O(n²) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/n² ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.

context_blocks.text: The input is small compared with the output. For X=(0,3) and Y=(1,4), the four indexed sums are 1,4,4,7. Both occurrences of 4 remain in the sorted output because they come from different pairs. In general there are n² output entries, but only 2n independent input numbers. This strong dependence is the reason ordinary sorting bounds for n² unrelated numbers may be wasteful.

If the two input lists are already sorted, the matrix M_ij=x_i+y_j increases along every row and every column. That information alone does not determine the relative order of every two cells: a later row may contain an entry smaller than an entry in an earlier row. Moreover, sum matrices satisfy additional equalities such as M_ij+M_kl=M_il+M_kj. The question concerns the full algebraic structure, not just arbitrary matrices with sorted rows and columns.

Explicitly generating and comparison-sorting all n² sums takes O(n² log n) time. Writing the required output already takes Ω(n²) operations, so quadratic time would match the output-size lower bound. TOPP identifies removal of the logarithmic factor as the main question. The real-valued input convention avoids assuming a small integer universe, where different operations can change the complexity.

Fredman proved that O(n²) comparisons suffice. A decision tree specifies the next comparison after every possible history of answers and places the sorted order at its leaves. Its depth counts comparisons, but it does not charge for constructing the tree or determining the next comparison from a succinct program. Consequently, a short decision tree does not automatically become an equally fast uniform algorithm.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu made the comparison savings algorithmic while retaining O(n² log n) total running time. This is a concrete separation between counting tests and charging the bookkeeping that organizes them. The target includes both costs, as well as all preprocessing and output writes.

Kane, Lovett and Moran later obtained O(n log² n) decision-tree depth by allowing tests involving differences of sums; each such linear test uses at most eight input coordinates. Those tests are more expressive than simply comparing two entries of X+Y. The subquadratic depth does not conflict with the quadratic output-size lower bound, because decision-tree depth does not charge for writing the output.

Related convolution problems ask only for a minimum, maximum or median on each antidiagonal of the sum matrix. These requests can have subquadratic algorithms without supplying a complete sorted list of all entries. The necklace-alignment paper explicitly records this distinction and the unresolved quadratic-time real-RAM question.

The importance of the question extends beyond sorting. Pairwise sums describe many ordered geometric events, and TOPP records reductions from this sorting task to polygon-containment and arrangement-ordering problems. A resolution would clarify how much algorithmic work can be saved when a large output is generated from a much smaller collection of numerical parameters.

cards.definitions: A hypergraph H=(V,E,w) has E⊆{e⊆V:|e|≥2} and weights w:E→ℝ_{≥0}. Its cut value is cut_H(S)=Σ_{e∈E: e∩S≠∅ and e∩(V\S)≠∅}w(e): a crossing hyperedge contributes its weight once, independently of how many of its vertices lie on either side. Zero-weight edges may be discarded; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. Empty or singleton hyperedges never cross a cut and are omitted without loss. H′=(V,E′,w′) follows the same conventions, with arbitrary nonnegative real weights. The output edge set E′ need not be a subset of E, following the original problem statement; new vertices are not permitted. Size means |E′|, not Σ_{e∈E′}|e|, weight-encoding length or total storage bits. C is independent of n, ε, edge count, rank and all weights. The empty edge set is allowed, and a zero input cut must remain exactly zero. This is a finite-object existence question: no construction algorithm, running-time or probability guarantee is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence statement with one constant C, or prove that the minimum required number of hyperedges times ε²/n is unbounded over the permitted inputs and accuracies. For a negative answer, the lower bound must allow arbitrary nonnegative hyperedges on the original vertex set. A growing logarithmic factor or a counterexample only to a particular sampling method does not resolve the target.

context_blocks.text: A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge {1,2,3,4} of weight one contributes one to both the partition {1}|{2,3,4} and the partition {1,2}|{3,4}. Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit O(n/ε²)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using O(n log n/ε²) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.
The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the Cn/ε² hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.

cards.title: Deterministic volume gap
cards.formal: For every locally checkable labeling problem Π on all finite graphs of some fixed maximum degree Δ, does the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm A with V_A(n)=o(n) imply the existence of a deterministic VOLUME algorithm B with V_B(n)=O(1+log* n)? Algorithms know the exact size of their input graph, and node identifiers are distinct integers in {1,…,|V(G)|²}. Here V_A(n) is the maximum number of distinct vertices visited to determine one vertex’s output, over all allowed instances with at most n vertices and all requested vertices.
cards.definitions: An LCL is specified by fixed Δ≥2, a fixed verification radius r≥1, finite nonempty input/output alphabets, and a finite set of permitted rooted radius-r labeled neighborhoods. Rules may inspect degrees and local ports, but not n or IDs. Instances include every finite nonempty simple undirected graph of maximum degree Δ, possibly disconnected, every input labeling and every port numbering. A labeling is valid exactly when all neighborhoods satisfy the rules. A deterministic VOLUME computation for a requested vertex v starts with v’s ID, degree, input, ports, Π and the exact |V(G)|, and visited set {v}. It may adaptively choose a visited vertex w and one of its incident ports, learning the neighbor u, its ID, degree, input and incident port names, then add u to the visited set. Arbitrary jumps to unseen IDs are forbidden. Only the number of distinct visited vertices, including v, is charged; local computation must terminate but its time and temporary space are unrestricted. Queries at different vertices run independently with no preprocessing or shared mutable state. Their outputs must jointly form a valid labeling for every input and ID assignment. Each algorithm is one finite computable program for all graph sizes. log* n is the number of iterated base-2 logarithms needed to reach at most 1; the added 1 handles small n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal implication, or specify one fixed LCL with a sublinear-volume deterministic algorithm and prove it has no O(log* n)-volume deterministic algorithm. Precisely, the latter lower bound means that for every correct B, every C>0 and every n₀, some n≥n₀ satisfies V_B(n)>C(1+log* n). This gap formulation fixes the asymptotic quantifiers without assuming an optimal algorithm or an arbitrary symbolic complexity function exists.
cards.why: This tests whether deterministic access to local solutions has only a tiny-information regime and an essentially global regime. Either outcome would substantially constrain the design and possible complexity classes of deterministic local computation algorithms.

importance.reason: A proposed collapse of an entire deterministic complexity interval, rather than a bound for one task. It clarifies the power of adaptive exploration and the role of randomness in local computation.

progress.text: Rosenbaum and Suomela introduce the distance-versus-volume framework and pose the deterministic intermediate-volume question as Question 7.1. Their examples establish several randomized intermediate scales while retaining linear deterministic volume.

Brandt, Grunau, and Rozhoň show that randomized local computation below o(√log n) can be sped up to deterministic O(log* n). Their results also give linear deterministic volume lower bounds for fixed-color tree-coloring tasks in the relevant bounded-degree setting. These do not cover every LCL.
Grunau, Rozhoň, and Brandt close the gap between constant and iterated-logarithmic VOLUME complexity. The much larger interval above log* n remains the issue here.
Suomela’s updated problem list retains the question of deterministic volume strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear.

Peng gives randomized VOLUME and LCA constructions of complexity Θ(log^k n) for positive integers k and polynomial scales up to logarithmic factors. Section 1.1 explicitly leaves the deterministic gap unresolved.

cards.status_note: The July 2026 primary paper explicitly retains the deterministic gap as open. The new constructions are randomized; no deterministic resolution located through 10 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: A processor that sees far through a narrow part of a graph can inspect much less information than one that explores an entire ball of the same radius. The VOLUME model measures that inspected information. Its adaptive exploration captures a central feature of answering a query about a huge graph without first constructing an entire solution.

Correctness still couples the answers. Independently determining the color or matching status of one vertex must agree with the answers obtained for every other vertex. The algorithm cannot save previous answers and use their accumulated state as a growing global solution. This makes a low-volume construction substantially stronger than an arbitrary sequential greedy algorithm.

Rosenbaum and Suomela ask whether there is any deterministic volume complexity strictly between iterated logarithmic and linear, and conjecture there is none. Their model supplies exact graph size and polynomially bounded identifiers. Removing these conventions changes the indistinguishability arguments, so the card keeps them explicit.

The known small-complexity gaps leave the central interval unresolved. Randomized examples inhabit many intermediate scales, but an algorithm that follows a favorable random exploration does not automatically give a deterministic procedure that succeeds on every labeled graph. A deterministic counterexample to the proposed collapse would establish a new basic behavior.

July 2026 work constructs additional randomized polylogarithmic and polynomial volume complexities. Its introduction explicitly separates those results from the still-open deterministic question. The increased richness on the randomized side makes the contrast sharper while supplying no deterministic intermediate example.

cards.title: Maximum independent set in the congested clique
cards.formal: Determine, up to constant factors as n grows, the optimal worst-case number $T_{\mathrm{MIS}}(n)$ of synchronous communication rounds needed to output an exact maximum independent set of an arbitrary simple undirected n-vertex graph in the deterministic unicast congested-clique model below. For every vertex v, its processor must output one bit indicating whether v belongs to the chosen set. Local computation and local storage are unrestricted; only communication rounds are charged. Here maximum means largest cardinality, not merely inclusion-wise maximal.
cards.definitions: There is one processor for each vertex in {1,...,n}. Initially every processor knows n, all processor identifiers, its own identifier, and exactly the edges incident to its vertex. The communication network is the complete graph regardless of which input edges exist. In each synchronous round, each processor may send a different message of at most $b=\max\{1,\lceil\log_2 n\rceil\}$ bits to each other processor; messages sent in a round become available at its end. Protocols are deterministic and must terminate correctly on every input. An independent set S contains no edge with both endpoints in S; maximum requires |S| >= |I| for every independent set I of the input graph. Define T_MIS(n) as the minimum round bound among protocols for n processors in this model. No polynomial bound is imposed on the computation between rounds. The deterministic and fixed-bandwidth conventions specialize the broader seminar question.
cards.answer_criterion: Give asymptotically matching upper and lower bounds: identify an explicit asymptotic function f(n), construct protocols taking O(f(n)) rounds on every graph, and prove that every correct deterministic protocol requires Omega(f(n)) rounds on some n-vertex graph for all sufficiently large n. Bounds separated by a logarithmic factor or a result only for maximal independent sets do not settle this target.
cards.why: This places a canonical exact graph optimization problem in a model where computation is free but communication is limited. Understanding its round complexity would help distinguish the benefit of distributing information from merely gathering the graph at one processor.

importance.reason: A canonical exact optimization task testing the communication power of the congested clique. Its relevance extends beyond symmetry breaking, although the chosen deterministic model is one specific frontier.

progress.text: Drucker, Kuhn, and Oshman establish circuit-simulation connections and distinguish unicast from broadcast congested cliques. Their work supplies model context, not a tight bound for the present task.

cards.status_note: The 2025 seminar source asks for the optimal round complexity. Searches through 10 September 2026 did not locate matching bounds for this exact task. Randomness and bandwidth are fixed explicitly here; results for maximal MIS, broadcast cliques, or edge-restricted CONGEST do not resolve this formulation.

context_blocks.text: The graph being optimized and the network carrying messages are different objects. Two vertices that are not adjacent in the input can still communicate directly. This removes distance as an obstacle while retaining a limit on how much information a processor can receive in one round. The task asks how much this distributed information limits exact optimization.

A simple baseline is to collect the entire graph at processor 1. Each other processor sends its n-bit adjacency row along its direct link, in blocks of b bits. These transmissions happen simultaneously and take O(n / log n) rounds for n >= 2. Processor 1 then enumerates subsets locally, chooses a largest independent set, and sends each processor its membership bit. This is an elementary upper bound for the stated model, rather than a claim that centralizing the graph is optimal.

The unlimited local computation is essential to interpreting this baseline. The exponential subset enumeration has no communication cost. Conversely, a faster centralized algorithm does not by itself reduce the number of rounds needed to assemble the input. The question isolates information movement from the ordinary running-time difficulty of exact independent set.

Lower bounds are especially delicate in the unicast clique. Drucker, Kuhn, and Oshman relate this model to powerful circuit computations, explaining why familiar sparse-network bottleneck arguments do not transfer directly. Chechik nevertheless identifies exact maximum independent set as a concrete round-complexity question. The catalogue has a separate constant-round question for a maximal independent set; that weaker output requirement must not be substituted here.

cards.title: LOCAL coloring below square-root degree dependence
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic LOCAL algorithm that properly colors every simple n-vertex graph of maximum degree $\Delta\ge2$ with colors in $\{1,\ldots,\Delta+1\}$ in $O(\Delta^{0.499}+\log^* n)$ synchronous rounds? Vertices have arbitrary distinct O(log n)-bit identifiers and know n and Delta. Messages along input edges and local computation are unbounded. The constant in the round bound must be independent of both n and Delta.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an algorithm with the specified uniform round bound, or prove that no deterministic LOCAL algorithm attains it. Improving a logarithmic factor while retaining degree exponent one-half does not meet the target.
cards.why: I include this because the familiar greedy palette bound hides a distinct distributed coordination problem. A fixed improvement in the degree exponent would reveal new ways to resolve local conflicts, while an impossibility result would explain why the square-root dependence persists across different coloring methods.
cards.definitions: Proper coloring means adjacent vertices receive different output colors. Delta denotes a supplied upper bound on degree, and the guarantee holds for every such valid bound. The algorithm is uniform over n, Delta, and identifier assignments. Log-star n is the number of repeated base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. Elapsed synchronous rounds are measured; this is not a sequential running-time or message-count target.

progress.text: Maus and Tonoyan obtain $O(\sqrt{\Delta\log\Delta}+\log^*n)$ deterministic rounds for the more general degree-plus-one list-coloring task. Ordinary coloring follows by using a common palette.
Suomela’s updated open-problem list explicitly asks whether the exponent 0.499 is attainable with Delta+1 colors and only an additive log-star n dependence.

The SODA 2026 discussion records a separate deterministic $\widetilde O(\log^{5/3}n)$ upper bound for Delta+1 coloring. That bound is independent of degree but does not provide the two-parameter guarantee asked here.

context_blocks.text: A sequential greedy algorithm needs only one more color than the maximum degree: when processing a vertex, at most Delta colors have already been used by its neighbors. In a distributed algorithm many adjacent vertices act simultaneously, so they can choose conflicting colors unless their decisions are coordinated.

Unique identifiers break perfect symmetry, but treating every identifier as a color starts with far too many colors. Color reduction has to compress this large palette while preserving a distinction across every edge. The degree controls how many simultaneous conflicts a vertex may need to avoid.

The two parameters in the target play different roles. Even when degree is fixed, the network can have arbitrarily many vertices, and iterated logarithmic time captures the unavoidable symmetry-breaking dependence on that size. An algorithm taking a power of log n cannot simply replace this term: for sufficiently large n, it exceeds every bound depending only on Delta plus log-star n.

The target chooses a specific exponent strictly below one-half, as in Suomela’s list. The numerical improvement is small; its purpose is to cross the apparent degree barrier while keeping the optimal-size palette. Allowing more colors, randomness, or a larger n-dependent term gives separate questions.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial linear programming
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic algorithm, with fixed polynomials p and q, that solves every rational linear program $\min\{c^Tx:Ax=b,\ x\ge0\}$, where A has m rows and n columns, using at most p(m+n) elementary arithmetic, comparison, and data-transfer operations, while every intermediate rational number has binary encoding length at most q(N)? Here N is the total input bit length. Solving means returning an exact optimal rational solution if one exists, or correctly reporting infeasibility or an objective unbounded below.
cards.definitions: A is in Q^(m by n), b in Q^m, and c in Q^n, with m,n>=1. All coefficients are supplied explicitly as binary signed numerators and positive denominators. No full-rank, nondegeneracy, strict-feasibility, coefficient-size, or conditioning promise is made. Elementary scalar operations are addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero quantity, comparisons, and transfers of stored values. The program is fixed and finite; no oracle, advice, randomization, floor operation, or uncharged access to binary digits is allowed. Rational encoding length means the bit length of a numerator-denominator representation. The polynomial p is independent of N and of every coefficient magnitude; q may depend on N. Consequently the algorithm must also admit a polynomial-time bit implementation. The output is a solution vector, not a required optimal basis. Infeasible means that the feasible set is empty; unbounded means it is nonempty and the infimum of c^T x is minus infinity. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This isolates whether the combinatorial dimensions of a linear program suffice to control its arithmetic complexity. A resolution would clarify the relation between numerical precision, polyhedral structure, and the complexity of one of optimization’s basic models.

importance.reason: A leading open question in optimization, separating ordinary polynomial-time solvability from a dimension-only arithmetic bound. Its reach includes general linear programming and many combinatorial optimization problems.

progress.text: The ellipsoid method and early interior-point algorithms establish polynomial-time solvability in the total input bit length. They do not provide a general strongly polynomial operation bound.

Tardos gives an algorithm whose arithmetic count is independent of the right-hand side and objective magnitudes, with remaining dependence on the constraint matrix. Small integer entries in that matrix give important strongly polynomial special cases.

Allamigeon, Gaubert, and Vandame construct LP families forcing exponentially many iterations for the self-concordant-barrier path-following methods covered by their theorem. This restricts a route to solving the problem; it is not an unrestricted LP lower bound.

Dadush, Koh, Natura, Olver, and Végh solve minimum-cost generalized flow and LPs with at most two nonzeros per row or column in strongly polynomial time. Their analysis also controls intermediate bit lengths.

Dadush, Ma, Natura, and Végh improve interior-point bounds in terms of straight-line complexity and give strongly polynomial trust-region subroutines. Straight-line complexity can itself be large, so these are not dimension-only bounds for arbitrary LPs.

Version 10 of Awoniyi’s preprint claims at most 2(m+n) complementary-pivot iterations for general LP. This review has not validated the termination/correctness argument and complete bit-complexity guarantee, and found no independent primary confirmation. The claim is not promoted to an established resolution.

context_blocks.text: Linear programming is already solvable in polynomial time when input length includes the bits used to write its coefficients. The unresolved issue is whether the number of arithmetic decisions can depend only on the number of constraints and variables. Very large capacities, costs, or denominators may require long arithmetic operands, but the question asks whether they must also force more arithmetic steps.

Both requirements in the definition are essential. Bounding the number of steps while allowing intermediate integers with exponentially many bits could hide enormous computation inside single arithmetic operations. Bounding only total bit time gives ordinary polynomial-time linear programming, which is already known. The strongly polynomial target combines a dimension-only operation count with controlled numerical representation.

Combinatorial optimization supplies positive examples. Tardos’s method removes dependence on the magnitudes of the right-hand side and objective, and yields strongly polynomial bounds for suitable small-coefficient constraint matrices. More recently, a strongly polynomial algorithm was obtained when each row, or each column, has at most two nonzero entries. These cases show that large numerical data alone need not force many arithmetic steps.

For unrestricted matrices, an algorithm may need a different way to navigate the feasible region. Long central paths can defeat broad classes of path-following methods, even though other approaches remain possible. A separate status issue is a 2025 preprint, revised in July 2026, claiming a general solution. Its claim is recorded below, but this review has not established its correctness or found independent validation.

cards.title: Log-squared query complexity for fixed-dimensional Tarski
cards.formal: Let Q(n,k) be the minimum worst-case number of adaptive deterministic value queries needed to find any fixed point of an unknown monotone function $f:[n]^k\to[n]^k$, where [n]={1,...,n} and monotonicity is with respect to coordinatewise order. A query at x reveals the entire vector f(x). Is it true that for every integer k>=1 there is a constant C_k such that $Q(n,k)\le C_k(1+\log_2 n)^2$ for every n>=2? Arbitrary finite computation between queries is allowed. Constants may depend on k but not on n or f. This asks for an exponent independent of the fixed dimension, not a polynomial bound on C_k.
cards.definitions: For x,y in the grid, x<=y means x_i<=y_i for every coordinate i. The oracle is promised to satisfy x<=y implies f(x)<=f(y). A valid output is any x with f(x)=x; no minimum or maximum fixed point is required. An adaptive query procedure can choose each query using all earlier queries and answers, and must terminate correctly for every promised oracle. Equivalently, Q(n,k) is the minimum depth of a finite deterministic oracle decision tree whose leaves output valid fixed points for every monotone function consistent with that leaf. Neither a circuit description nor the table of f is part of the input. Query cost is one per returned vector, and places no restriction on the bit complexity of choosing the next query. The finite product grid is a complete lattice, so a fixed point always exists.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the bound for every fixed k, or show that there is a fixed k for which Q(n,k)/(1+log_2 n)^2 is unbounded as n grows. A growing factor depending only on k is permitted. A bound whose logarithmic exponent grows with k does not answer yes. A lower bound obtained only by letting k grow with n does not answer no unless it implies failure at some fixed k.
cards.why: This probes the information cost of finding a guaranteed fixed point under monotonicity, a basic organizing principle in algorithms, semantics, and equilibrium computation. The same sharp bound in dimensions two, three, and four makes the dependence on dimension a substantive structural mystery rather than just a loose analysis of one algorithm.

importance.reason: A broad oracle-complexity question about monotone fixed points, with a surprising low-dimensional pattern and connections to equilibrium search. It distinguishes intrinsic information requirements from implementation time.

progress.text: Etessami, Papadimitriou, Rubinstein, and Yannakakis prove an Omega(log^2 n) lower bound already in two dimensions, including for randomized algorithms; the 2022 seminar records this starting point.

Brânzei, Phillips, and Recker prove randomized query lower bound Omega(k log^2 n / log k) for n,k>=2. For fixed k this remains quadratic in log n, so it does not rule out the card’s target.

Chen, Li, and Yannakakis obtain O(log^2 n) queries in four dimensions and improve the exponent in every fixed dimension. Section 9 proposes the possibility of a generic dimension-dependent constant times log^2 n.

context_blocks.text: Starting at the bottom of the grid and repeatedly applying f gives a nondecreasing chain until a fixed point is reached. This directly proves existence constructively, but the chain can contain a number of steps proportional to n times the dimension. Since the coordinates need only log n bits to describe, dependence on n can be exponentially larger than dependence on the coordinate description length.

One-dimensional search can exploit order by repeatedly discarding a large interval. In a product order, two points can be incomparable: one coordinate is larger and another smaller. The oracle’s monotonicity then does not directly compare their images. The question asks whether these multidimensional interactions must eventually increase the power of log n, or whether they can be absorbed into a dimension-dependent constant.

The first surprise was that dimensions two and three both have Theta(log^2 n) query complexity. Chen, Li, and Yannakakis extend this equality to dimension four in their March 2026 preprint. Their more general upper bound is O(log^(ceil((k-1)/3)+1) n) for fixed k. The concluding discussion explicitly raises a bound of the form f(k) log^2 n, which is the target on this card.

Query complexity and computational efficiency must be separated here. The 2026 algorithm uses expensive intermediate search and counting; its authors leave a time-efficient implementation open. Even a positive answer to this card would only limit how much oracle information is needed. Obtaining a polynomial-time algorithm when both k and log n are input parameters would require additional control of the constants and the work between queries.

cards.title: Planar k-set problem
cards.formal: Let K₂(n,k) be the maximum, over sets P of n distinct points in $\mathbb R^2$ with no three collinear, of the number of distinct subsets S⊆P of size k strictly separable from P\S by a line. Determine K₂(n,k) up to universal constant factors, uniformly for all integers n≥2 and 1≤k≤⌊n/2⌋.
cards.definitions: Strict separation means that there are real a,b,c with (a,b)≠(0,0), ax+by<c for every (x,y)∈S, and ax+by>c for every (x,y)∈P\S. The objects counted are subsets S, not their infinitely many possible separating lines. Coordinates have no bounded-precision, grid, or random-distribution promise. The target is worst-case combinatorial complexity, not the running time of an enumeration algorithm. A matching bound means an asymptotic expression F(n,k) and absolute constants 0<c₀≤C₀<∞ such that c₀F(n,k)≤K₂(n,k)≤C₀F(n,k) throughout the stated range, apart from finitely many n which can be absorbed into the constants. Bounds must cover k that grows with n. Complementation supplies the remaining values n/2<k<n; k=0,n each have one subset. This card specializes the original all-dimensions problem to the plane.

An answer representation must be selected before this is a closed benchmark specification.

context_blocks.text: A line can realize only a small fraction of all choices of k points. The question measures the combinatorial capacity of one linear cut at a fixed output size. For example, when k=1 the separable points are the convex-hull vertices, and their maximum number is n. The difficult regime lets k increase with the input size.

Point-line duality translates changes of a separating line into the structure of levels in a line arrangement. A level tracks positions having a specified number of lines below them. These level bounds recur in geometric selection and in analyses of parametric optimization. Dey’s method also yields bounds for related level structures, convex chains, and parametric spanning-tree problems.

For even n, the balanced case is closely tied to halving edges: segments joining two input points whose supporting line leaves (n−2)/2 of the other points on each side. A halving edge is not itself a separating line, since it passes through input points. The correspondence between k-sets and directed (k−1)-edges gives K₂(n,n/2) equal to twice the maximum number of undirected halving edges.

The known planar upper bound is O(n k^(1/3)), whereas constructions give n exp(Ω(√log k)) subsets. In the balanced regime the latter grows faster than n times any fixed power of log n, yet slower than n^(1+ε) for each fixed ε>0. Thus neither a linear bound nor an ordinary polylogarithmic correction to linear growth can describe the worst case.

Sharper finite-size constructions and improvements to the additive terms of halving-line bounds are useful progress. They do not close the gap in asymptotic growth. Keeping this distinction explicit matters here: an improved upper bound may retain the same 4/3 exponent in the balanced case.

Point-line duality translates changes of a separating line into the structure of levels in a line arrangement. A level tracks positions having a specified number of lines below them. These level bounds recur in geometric selection and in analyses of parametric optimization. Dey’s method also yields bounds for related level structures, convex chains, and parametric spanning-tree problems.

For even n, the balanced case is closely tied to halving edges: segments joining two input points whose supporting line leaves (n−2)/2 of the other points on each side. A halving edge is not itself a separating line, since it passes through input points. The correspondence between k-sets and directed (k−1)-edges gives K₂(n,n/2) equal to twice the maximum number of undirected halving edges.

The known planar upper bound is O(n k^(1/3)), whereas constructions give n exp(Ω(√log k)) subsets. In the balanced regime the latter grows faster than n times any fixed power of log n, yet slower than n^(1+ε) for each fixed ε>0. Thus neither a linear bound nor an ordinary polylogarithmic correction to linear growth can describe the worst case.

Sharper finite-size constructions and improvements to the additive terms of halving-line bounds are useful progress. They do not close the gap in asymptotic growth. Keeping this distinction explicit matters here: an improved upper bound may retain the same 4/3 exponent in the balanced case.

cards.title: One-way functions from P ≠ NP
cards.formal: Does P≠NP imply that there exists a deterministic polynomial-time computable function f:{0,1}*→{0,1}* such that, for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithm I and every constant c>0, all sufficiently large n satisfy $\Pr_{x\sim U_n,\,I}[\,|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)\,]\le n^{-c}$, where $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$?
cards.definitions: Uₙ is the uniform distribution on n-bit strings. The function f is computed by one deterministic Turing machine in worst-case polynomial time; in particular its output length is polynomially bounded in n. The inverter receives n in unary and the output f(x), uses independent unbiased random bits, and runs in worst-case polynomial time in the length of its input on every random tape. Its output may be an n-bit candidate or failure. Finding any n-bit preimage counts as success, not only recovering the original x. The probability includes both the choice of x and the inverter’s coins. Formally, for every fixed inverter I and real c>0 there exists N(I,c) such that the inequality holds for every n≥N(I,c). This is eventual negligible inversion probability, not security only at infinitely many lengths. Algorithms have no oracle, nonuniform advice, trapdoor, or quantum computation. The premise P≠NP concerns ordinary uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision versus polynomial-time verification. The task is an existence implication and does not require a black-box construction or a particular proof method.

context_blocks.text: If P=NP, an inverter can search for a preimage one bit at a time. At each step, it asks whether the current prefix can be extended to an n-bit string mapping to the given output. That is an NP question because a full preimage is a short efficiently checked certificate. Thus one-way functions imply P≠NP. The missing direction is whether worst-case difficulty alone supplies the required average-case inversion hardness.

A hard instance somewhere is insufficient for security. A polynomial-time inverter might succeed on nearly every output generated from a uniform input and fail only on an extremely rare set. One-wayness must rule out even inverse-polynomial overall success. The distribution is induced by evaluating f on uniform x; requiring hardness on uniformly random output strings would be a different condition, particularly when f has uneven preimage sizes.

One-way functions have unusually broad consequences despite their simple definition. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby prove that they suffice for pseudorandom generators, with the converse also holding. This makes the question a foundation for computational pseudorandomness and basic cryptographic constructions. Public-key encryption or a trapdoor for inversion would impose additional requirements beyond the target here.

Known barriers constrain certain attempts to turn an arbitrary NP-hard problem into a secure function by oracle reductions. They do not rule out constructions that use more structure or different proof methods. Separating a limitation of a reduction from a negative answer to the mathematical implication is essential.

The 2026 work of Liu and Pass relates one-way functions to boundary hardness of time-bounded description complexity. For the ordinary deterministic description-length formulation, their characterization retains an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. This is progress on specific sources of cryptographic hardness, but the premise is not merely P≠NP.

cards.definitions: [n]={1,…,n}. An access structure Γ⊆2^[n] is monotone when A∈Γ and A⊆B⊆[n] imply B∈Γ. A scheme is a joint probability distribution of a secret B uniform on {0,1} and shares X_i∈S_i, where each S_i is a finite nonempty set. For each A∈Γ there is a deterministic map r_A:∏_{i∈A}S_i→{0,1} such that r_A((X_i)_{i∈A})=B with probability one. For each A∉Γ, the conditional distributions of (X_i)_{i∈A} given B=0 and B=1 are identical. This is exact reconstruction and perfect information-theoretic privacy, with arbitrary collusion within A. Share size is the base-two logarithm of its alphabet cardinality, not its Shannon entropy or the sum over participants. It is normalized by the secret size of one bit. There is no linearity, field, threshold, computation-time or uniform construction requirement. The scheme may depend on the whole finite access structure. K,c must be universal. Rounding log₂|S_i| up to an integer encoding length changes K only by an absolute factor.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Nir’s August 2026 preprint states a directly matching positive result. Theorem 1.5 gives every n-party access structure a scheme for a one-bit secret with maximal share size 2^{0.496n+o(n)}. Taking any fixed c between 0.496 and 1/2 absorbs the sublinear exponent for large n; a universal K covers the finitely many smaller sizes. The proof has not been independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

An access structure describes which groups may reconstruct a secret. It need not depend only on group size: a designated participant may be essential, or several different combinations may be authorized. Monotonicity means that an authorized group stays authorized when more participants join. Perfect privacy requires even an unlimited observer holding every share of an unauthorized group to see the same distribution for either secret value.

For example, suppose participant 1 together with either participant 2 or participant 3 may reconstruct a bit B. Choose an independent uniform bit R and give shares R, B XOR R, B XOR R respectively. Either authorized pair recovers B by XOR. Participants 2 and 3 together see two copies of a uniform masked bit and learn nothing about B; participant 1 alone sees independent randomness. This simple access structure needs only one bit per share, but arbitrary patterns can be much harder.

The question concerns the largest participant’s stored alphabet, measured in bits. A share with M possible values costs log₂ M, even if its probability distribution has smaller entropy. The total share size is between the largest share and n times that share; these measures have the same leading exponential rate. None of these conventions permits replacing perfect privacy by computational secrecy or small statistical leakage.

The classical construction treats authorized sets separately and can use exponentially large shares. Successive results reduced the exponent; Applebaum and Nir’s 2021 bound is 1.5^{n+o(n)}, equivalently 2^{0.58496…n+o(n)}. This remains above the half exponent requested in the seminar question. The seminar list prints a different earlier upper exponent; the primary construction is used for the historical bound recorded here.

Linearity is a real restriction: shares are linear combinations of the secret and random field elements. Known exponential lower bounds for linear schemes do not apply to all joint distributions allowed in this card. Likewise, lower bounds for particular reconstruction degrees or graph access structures need their own hypotheses. A general upper bound must handle every monotone authorized-group pattern, with one universal exponent.

The same 2026 preprint gives a half-exponent linear construction and a strictly smaller nonlinear exponent. Its nonlinear theorem is the part relevant to this card; the linear theorem alone would not satisfy c<1/2.

cards.title: BPP versus BQP
cards.formal: Is $\mathrm{BPP}\subsetneq\mathrm{BQP}$? Equivalently, is there a total decision language L⊆{0,1}* with a uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm that is correct with probability at least 2/3 on every input, but no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time classical algorithm with the same per-input correctness guarantee?
cards.definitions: BPP uses a single classical probabilistic Turing machine with independent unbiased coins, worst-case time C(n+1)^k on n-bit inputs, and error probability at most 1/3 separately for every input. BQP uses a polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum circuits: a deterministic classical machine on 1ⁿ generates the circuit description in polynomial time. Fix gates H, T, and CNOT, where H is the Hadamard gate, T=diag(1,exp(iπ/4)), and CNOT is controlled bit-flip. Gates may act on any addressed qubits. The input register starts in |x⟩, polynomially many auxiliary qubits start in |0⟩, and one designated qubit is measured in the computational basis at the end. Its output must equal the membership bit with probability at least 2/3 for every x. The family has no advice, oracle gates, postselection, or arbitrary real-number gate parameters. Size and register bounds use fixed polynomial exponents independent of n. Equivalent standard uniform quantum-machine definitions give the same class. The problem concerns one-bit decisions on all binary strings, with no promise on the input. It does not ask for exact amplitudes, full output distributions, or a separation restricted to shallow classical circuits.

cards.why: This is the basic complexity-theoretic question of whether quantum computation expands the set of efficiently decidable problems beyond classical randomization. It gives a precise target behind the broader phrase quantum advantage and distinguishes unrestricted computational power from experimentally or structurally restricted demonstrations.

importance.reason: A central foundational separation between classical and quantum efficient computation, with consequences for algorithms, simulation, and the computational interpretation of quantum mechanics.

context_blocks.text: Quantum computation uses interference between amplitudes, while a randomized classical algorithm evolves a probability distribution. Both models on this card ultimately output one ordinary bit with bounded error. Efficient classical random computation can be embedded in a quantum circuit, so the question is whether interference provides a strict advantage for some decision problem when both sides receive unrestricted polynomial time.

Shor’s algorithms give polynomial-time quantum factoring and discrete logarithms. They are compelling candidate advantages because efficient classical algorithms for these tasks are not known. Their classical intractability has not been proved, so the quantum algorithms alone do not separate BPP from BQP. Moreover, these are naturally function problems; a class separation still needs an appropriate decision language and a classical lower bound.

Oracle results demonstrate a stronger separation in a different setting. Raz and Tal construct an oracle relative to which BQP is not contained even in the polynomial hierarchy. In that model, an oracle call accesses a specially chosen function at unit cost, including coherently for the quantum machine. Replacing that oracle by an explicit efficiently implemented input computation is an additional requirement, not part of the oracle theorem.

There are also unconditional advantages against restricted classical circuits. Bene Watts and Parham’s August 2026 publication separates constant-depth quantum sampling from specified bounded-fan-in classical sampling models, including a restriction on available random inputs in its uniform result. This establishes an actual lower bound in that model. It leaves open arbitrary-depth polynomial-time classical decision procedures.

Even the equality BPP=BQP would assert efficient simulation only of the decision tasks defining these classes. A demand to reproduce every quantum output distribution or calculate every amplitude to high precision can be computationally stronger. Keeping the output requirement explicit prevents those simulation problems from being mistaken for this one.

cards.title: P versus BPP
cards.formal: Does P=BPP? Precisely, for every language L for which a randomized Turing machine R runs in polynomial time on every input and every random tape, and satisfies $\Pr[R(x)=1_L(x)]\ge2/3$ for every binary string x, does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine deciding L correctly on every x? The polynomial time bound of the deterministic machine may depend on R.
cards.definitions: Input length is n=|x|. A polynomial-time bound means C(n+1)^k steps for fixed constants C,k, independent of x and of the random bits. R uses independent unbiased random bits, at most one fresh bit per computation step, and outputs a single bit. Its error may be on either yes or no inputs, but is bounded separately on each input. P consists of deterministic polynomial-time decision languages and BPP of languages meeting the randomized guarantee above. These are total decision problems, with no excluded promise inputs. No advice, oracle, quantum operations, or input distribution is allowed. The requested deterministic simulation may use a different algorithm; it need not reproduce R's random choices, preserve its precise exponent, or be generated by an effective compiler from R.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This determines whether random bits add power to efficient total decision computation. It is a central organizing question for pseudorandom generators, explicit constructions, and the connection between circuit lower bounds and algorithm design.

importance.reason: The main general derandomization question for polynomial-time decision algorithms, with broad consequences for the role of randomness and for hardness-versus-randomness techniques.

progress.text: Adleman establishes BPP⊆P/poly. Suitable fixed random advice exists for each input length, but uniform polynomial-time computation of that advice is not supplied.

Impagliazzo and Wigderson prove P=BPP if there is a Boolean function computable in time 2^(O(n)) that requires circuits of size 2^(c n), for some c>0 and all sufficiently large n. The circuit-hardness assumption remains essential to this theorem.

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh, and Zuckerman improve conditional pseudorandomness parameters for algorithms satisfying an insensitivity property of their correct and incorrect random tapes. This concerns finer generators for a specified algorithm class, not unconditional removal of randomness from all BPP computations.

Version 9 of a preprint by Tianrong Lin claims the opposite conclusion P≠BPP, along with stronger separations. This review has not verified that construction or located independent primary validation. The claimed separation is recorded without treating it as established.
