context_blocks.text: Randomized decision algorithms may use randomness to avoid exceptional choices or to test a property through a small sample. Their guarantee is pointwise: even the worst input must receive the correct answer with high probability. Repeating an algorithm reduces its error but leaves it randomized. The question asks whether every such use of randomness can ultimately be replaced by a deterministic polynomial computation.

Exhaustive majority evaluation over all random tapes has a time cost exponential in their length. That is correct, but takes exponential time when the tape has polynomial length. A suitable pseudorandom generator would reduce the search to a polynomial-size set of tapes, constructed efficiently. The hard part is ensuring that this small set fools the computation on every input.

A nonuniform version of this idea already works: after error amplification, an averaging argument supplies one polynomial-length advice string that works for every input of a given length. This proves BPP is contained in P/poly. The string can depend on the input length without an efficient procedure to find it, which is exactly why that inclusion does not answer the uniform question.

Strong circuit hardness provides a conditional route to full derandomization. Impagliazzo and Wigderson show that an exponentially circuit-hard function computable in exponential time suffices. The condition is substantially more specific than merely P≠NP. Current work also studies the amount of slowdown and the structure of the randomized algorithm, producing finer conditional results without an unconditional equality proof.

This card concerns computing one correct decision bit. Sampling a distribution, producing one of many valid witnesses, or deciding only inputs with a promise leads to related but different formulations. Keeping these tasks separate prevents a derandomization theorem for one setting from being silently substituted for another.

cards.title: L versus BPL
cards.formal: Is L=BPL? Equivalently, for every language S⊆{0,1}* decided with two-sided error at most 1/3 by a uniform randomized Turing machine using O(log(n+2)) work space and polynomial time on inputs of length n, is there a uniform deterministic Turing machine deciding S with O(log(n+2)) work space?
cards.definitions: The machines have a finite description, a read-only two-way input tape, and a fixed finite number of work tapes over a fixed finite alphabet. Space counts all visited work-tape cells; the input tape is excluded. A randomized machine receives independent fair coin outcomes one at a time, without a freely rereadable random tape: an outcome must be stored in counted work space to be remembered. It halts with ACCEPT or REJECT on every input and every random tape within K(n+2)^c steps and uses at most K log_2(n+2) work cells, for some constants K,c depending only on the machine. For each input x, acceptance probability is at least 2/3 if x∈S and at most 1/3 if x∉S. This is a language problem with no promise excluding intermediate-probability inputs. A deterministic decider must halt and give the correct answer on every input; any halting deterministic logarithmic-space decider has polynomially many configurations and hence polynomial running time. Both classes are uniform and have no advice. The deterministic machine and its space constant may depend on S. The equality does not demand a computable compiler transforming arbitrary machine descriptions, nor a particular pseudorandom-generator construction.

context_blocks.text: A logarithmic-space computation can maintain indices and counters while remembering only a small part of the input. Randomness lets it explore many possible choices without storing all of them. The equality asks whether this apparent extra power disappears when the required output is only a bounded-error decision about the input.

The memory convention is central. Fresh random outcomes can be read once; a machine cannot revisit an arbitrarily long random string without paying for its storage or reconstructing it. Conversely, the deterministic simulator is allowed a different constant in its logarithmic-space bound. The question concerns equality of language classes, not identical execution traces.

Saks and Zhou gave a deterministic simulation using O(log^(3/2) n) space. Hoza improved the bound to O(log^(3/2) n / sqrt(log log n)), with the expression understood asymptotically. These bounds are substantially below squared logarithmic space but remain above a constant multiple of log n.

The 2026 work of Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma improves error reduction for weighted pseudorandom generators. Its revised account distinguishes weighted generators from ordinary generators and attributes the relevant arity/error connection to Cheng and Hoza. Those parameter improvements do not establish the equality of classes asked here.

The catalogue separately contains a concrete optimal-generator problem for read-once branching programs. Such a construction can have consequences for logarithmic-space derandomization, but the language-class equality does not prescribe that particular construction. This completed card retains the original TCS-0026 identity and Wigderson reference while making the computation and error models explicit.

cards.title: Unique Games Conjecture
cards.area: Approximation algorithms and hardness of approximation
cards.formal: For every pair of rational constants ε,δ>0 with ε+δ<1, does there exist an integer q≥2 such that it is NP-hard to distinguish Unique Games instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\ge1-\varepsilon$ from instances with $\operatorname{val}(G)\le\delta$? Here q is the alphabet size, fixed independently of the input graph, and val(G) is the largest fraction of constraints simultaneously satisfied by any labeling.
cards.definitions: An instance has finitely many vertices and a nonempty explicit list E of directed edges between distinct vertices; repeated edges are allowed and counted separately. Every vertex receives a label in [q]={1,…,q}. An edge e=(u,v) carries an explicitly given permutation π_e:[q]→[q] and is satisfied exactly when π_e(ℓ(u))=ℓ(v). Thus val(G)=max_ℓ |{e satisfied by ℓ}|/|E|. There are no graph expansion or degree promises. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3SAT mapping every satisfiable formula into the ≥1−ε case and every unsatisfiable formula into the ≤δ case. The reduction, its running-time exponent, and q may depend on ε,δ. Inputs with value strictly between the thresholds are outside the promise. The question is the NP-hardness proposition itself; P≠NP is needed when drawing the usual conclusion that no polynomial-time distinguishing algorithm exists. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: UGC would turn many conditional approximation thresholds into NP-hardness theorems and explain the optimality of a general SDP framework. Its very simple permutation constraints isolate a fundamental boundary between exact consistency, approximate consistency, and hardness amplification.

importance.reason: An organizing conjecture for approximation thresholds, with consequences for whole families of constraint satisfaction problems and strong connections to SDP algorithms, PCPs, and analysis.

progress.text: Khot proposes the conjecture. Perfect satisfiability is polynomial-time decidable; the conjectured hard regime has positive completeness error and an alphabet depending on both gap parameters.

Raghavendra gives a general SDP and rounding framework for fixed finite-domain CSPs and transfers SDP integrality gaps to Unique-Games-based hardness. Under UGC, its achievable thresholds are optimal up to any fixed accuracy, unless P=NP.

Arora, Barak, and Steurer give, for an absolute α>0, an exp(q n^(ε^α))-time algorithm finding a (1−ε^α)-satisfying labeling in a (1−ε)-satisfiable q-label instance on n vertices. In the small fixed-ε regime this is subexponential, but not polynomial.

The line of work proving the 2-to-2 Games Theorem yields NP-hardness of Unique Games at completeness 1/2 and arbitrarily small soundness. Khot’s exposition states this explicitly as Theorem 2.20; it leaves the near-one completeness of UGC unresolved.

The journal version of Dinur, Khot, Kindler, Minzer, and Safra’s second installment documents its role in the proof sequence, while retaining the full Unique Games statement as Conjecture 1.4. Its publication is not a new proof of full UGC.

context_blocks.text: Each constraint is locally simple: fixing either endpoint label determines exactly one compatible label at the other endpoint. Exact satisfiability of all constraints is decidable in polynomial time. Allowing a small fraction of constraints to fail changes the question sharply.

The conjecture says that an instance admitting an almost perfect assignment can nevertheless be hard to distinguish from one where every assignment fails almost everywhere. These are two promised regimes, rather than a request to compute the exact optimum. The alphabet is allowed to grow as the desired gap becomes more demanding. Indeed, a uniformly random labeling satisfies a 1/q fraction in expectation, so a soundness threshold below 1/q is impossible.

Raghavendra’s theorem connects such reductions to a general semidefinite-programming framework: under UGC, that framework achieves the approximation thresholds of fixed finite-domain constraint satisfaction problems, to arbitrary constant accuracy.

The strongest relevant hardness milestone must be read with its completeness parameter. The 2-to-2 Games Theorem implies hardness for Unique Games with value at least one half versus arbitrarily small value. It does not make the yes instances almost perfectly satisfiable. Raising completeness from one half to arbitrarily close to one is precisely a remaining gap relevant to this card.

Algorithmic progress also matters even when it is slower than polynomial time. Subexponential algorithms exploit spectral decompositions of the constraint graph, limiting what quantitative hardness reductions could establish. Because a polynomial reduction can enlarge the instance by a parameter-dependent power, these algorithms coexist with the NP-hardness conjecture.

cards.title: Average-case NP hardness from P ≠ NP
cards.formal: Is the implication $\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\Longrightarrow(\mathrm{NP},\mathrm{PSamp})\nsubseteq\mathrm{AvgP}$ true? That is, assuming P≠NP, must there exist a language L∈NP and a polynomial-time samplable distribution ensemble D={Dₙ} such that no deterministic exact decider for L runs in average polynomial time under D, in the moment-based sense defined below?
cards.definitions: A sampler is one randomized Turing machine S which, given 1ⁿ, halts within q(n) steps on every random tape for a fixed polynomial q. Its output distribution Dₙ is over finite binary strings x; |x|≤q(n), and n is the ensemble parameter, not necessarily |x|. Sampling is exact with independent unbiased coin flips, and S has no advice or oracle. An exact decider A receives (1ⁿ,x), halts, and returns the membership bit of L correctly for every n and x. Write T_A(1ⁿ,x) for its running time. The pair (L,D) belongs to AvgP if there exist such an A, ε>0, C>0, and integer k≥1 with $\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\varepsilon]\le C(n+1)^k$ for every n≥1. The constants and A may depend on L and S but not on n. This moment definition is the robust Levin notion, not the requirement that the first moment itself be polynomial. The algorithm is deterministic and never gives a wrong answer; difficult inputs may take a long time. NP uses ordinary polynomially bounded certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification. Both the hard language and its sampler must be fixed across all input lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This asks whether worst-case intractability necessarily survives on inputs generated by a feasible process. It is the basic bridge between the standard theory of NP-completeness and distributional complexity, and a prerequisite issue in attempts to derive useful cryptographic hardness from P≠NP alone.

importance.reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.

progress.text: Levin develops robust average-time definitions and distributional completeness; Impagliazzo and Levin extend completeness to samplable ensembles. The survey develops the moment definition and this completeness theory.

Bogdanov and Trevisan show limitations of nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP. Their result is a conditional obstruction to a reduction method, not a disproof of the unrestricted implication.
Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.5 and the revised Bogdanov–Trevisan survey explicitly ask whether P≠NP implies average-case NP hardness.

Liu and Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case reduction for an exact time-bounded Kolmogorov problem under an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. The extra hypothesis is stronger and more specific than P≠NP.

cards.status_note: The original question is explicitly open in Wigderson’s book and the revised average-case survey. Current primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no resolution from P≠NP alone was located. The card fixes deterministic exact AvgP and strict polynomial-time sampling, rather than conflating them with randomized heuristic hardness.

context_blocks.text: Worst-case hardness says that an algorithm has difficult inputs. It does not say that a feasible instance generator produces them with enough probability to obstruct average efficiency. The sampler is therefore part of the mathematical problem. It may depend on the language, but it cannot contain an uncomputable table selecting a hard input at every length.

A padding example shows why a fixed familiar distribution is insufficient. Encode a formula x as 0 followed by |x|²−1 further zeros, a separator 1, and x. Satisfiability of these padded strings remains NP-complete under polynomial reductions. Under the uniform distribution on strings of a fixed length, valid encodings are so rare that checking the format and brute-forcing the rare valid formulas has polynomial average cost. An easy uniform distribution does not remove worst-case hardness.

Levin’s moment condition makes average efficiency stable under polynomial slowdowns. If a machine is simulated with its running time raised to a fixed power, a correspondingly smaller positive moment still suffices. This prevents the answer from depending on an incidental choice of machine representation. Exact computation with this runtime guarantee differs from a heuristic allowed to give incorrect answers on a small fraction of inputs.

Distributional completeness is already available: Impagliazzo and Levin extend the theory to polynomial-time samplable ensembles. Completeness identifies a common average-case target; it does not prove that this target is hard from P≠NP.

There are barriers for nonadaptive oracle reductions from worst-case NP hardness to average-case NP hardness: the relevant reductions would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such a barrier leaves other proof mechanisms open. Recent reductions for specific time-bounded Kolmogorov problems use additional assumptions or specific forms of hardness, so they do not supply the implication on this card.

category_assignment.reason: Average-case complexity and hardness

sentences: Worst-case NP hardness means that some efficiently verifiable problem resists polynomial-time solution on all inputs.
The question asks whether P unequal to NP forces such a problem to remain hard on average under an efficiently samplable distribution.
The hard instances must occur often enough in a distribution that can itself be generated feasibly.
A positive implication would connect worst-case complexity with the distributional hardness needed in many algorithmic and cryptographic settings.
The reviewed target uses deterministic exact decisions and Levin's moment-based average-time definition, which differs from allowing errors on rare inputs or requiring only a polynomial first moment.

cards.context:
Worst-case hardness says that an algorithm has difficult inputs. It does not say that a feasible instance generator produces them with enough probability to obstruct average efficiency. The sampler is therefore part of the mathematical problem. It may depend on the language, but it cannot contain an uncomputable table selecting a hard input at every length.

A padding example shows why a fixed familiar distribution is insufficient. Encode a formula x as 0 followed by |x|²−1 further zeros, a separator 1, and x. Satisfiability of these padded strings remains NP-complete under polynomial reductions. Under the uniform distribution on strings of a fixed length, valid encodings are so rare that checking the format and brute-forcing the rare valid formulas has polynomial average cost. An easy uniform distribution does not remove worst-case hardness.

Levin’s moment condition makes average efficiency stable under polynomial slowdowns. If a machine is simulated with its running time raised to a fixed power, a correspondingly smaller positive moment still suffices. This prevents the answer from depending on an incidental choice of machine representation. Exact computation with this runtime guarantee differs from a heuristic allowed to give incorrect answers on a small fraction of inputs.

Distributional completeness is already available: Impagliazzo and Levin extend the theory to polynomial-time samplable ensembles. Completeness identifies a common average-case target; it does not prove that this target is hard from P≠NP.

There are barriers for nonadaptive oracle reductions from worst-case NP hardness to average-case NP hardness: the relevant reductions would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such a barrier leaves other proof mechanisms open. Recent reductions for specific time-bounded Kolmogorov problems use additional assumptions or specific forms of hardness, so they do not supply the implication on this card.

cards.title: 3-colorability of diameter-two graphs
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every finite simple connected undirected graph G of diameter at most 2, decides whether there is a map c:V(G)→{1,2,3} such that c(u)≠c(v) for every edge uv?
cards.definitions: The input is the adjacency matrix of an n-vertex graph. Distance counts edges in a shortest path, and diameter is the maximum distance between any two vertices. The graph has no loops or parallel edges. For a singleton the diameter is 0. The algorithm must correctly decide existence of a coloring, including on graphs that are not 3-colorable; it is not supplied with a coloring or a promise of 3-colorability. The color set has fixed size three and there are no vertex lists, precolored vertices, degree bounds, or forbidden-subgraph assumptions. A polynomial-time algorithm has worst-case running time C(n+1)^k for constants C,k independent of G. One may equivalently define a total language that rejects disconnected or diameter-greater-than-two graphs, since the diameter promise can be checked in polynomial time. Restricting to diameter exactly two gives the same polynomial-time question: diameter-zero and diameter-one connected graphs are complete and their colorability is immediate.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that such an algorithm exists, or that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-completeness proof would establish the conventional hardness classification and imply a negative answer under P≠NP. A subexponential algorithm or an algorithm requiring an additional graph restriction does not settle this question.
cards.why: Three-colorability is a basic constraint-satisfaction problem, and diameter is one of the simplest measures of graph connectivity. This single unresolved boundary tests whether very short distances enforce exploitable structure without any sparsity assumption. Either an algorithm or a hardness reduction would explain a fundamental limit of structural restrictions in graph algorithms.

importance.reason: A longstanding concrete tractability boundary for a canonical NP-complete problem: two colors and diameter one are easy, while three colors at diameter three are hard. It supports the broader study of algorithms on structurally restricted graphs.

progress.text: Mertzios and Spirakis obtain a 2^{O(sqrt(n log n))} algorithm for diameter two and NP-completeness for diameter three, including triangle-free inputs.
Paulusma records the diameter-two three-color question as the exceptional unresolved (number of colors, diameter) pair.
Dębski, Piecyk, and Rzążewski improve the diameter-two upper bound to $2^{O(n^{1/3} \log^2 n)}$. Their abstract states that polynomial-time solvability remains open.
Murakami proves polynomial-time list 3-coloring for graphs of diameter two with no four-cycle as a subgraph. Sections 1 and 7 leave unrestricted diameter-two 3-colorability open.

context_blocks.text: The 2019 source discusses several diameter-restricted coloring problems. This card selects its central explicit question, with three colors and diameter two. The same section also asks about triangle-free inputs and about coloring claw-free graphs with an input-dependent number of colors; these are distinct extensions, not additional requirements hidden in this question.

Bounding diameter means every pair of vertices is close, but it does not bound the amount of global information encoded by the graph. Diameter-one graphs are complete and trivial to color. Mertzios and Spirakis show that 3-colorability is already NP-complete at diameter three, even for triangle-free graphs. Diameter two is the remaining boundary between these neighboring cases.

A tempting hardness reduction adds a universal vertex to an arbitrary graph. This makes the diameter at most two, but the new vertex consumes a color that none of the old vertices can use. It transfers general 3-colorability to 4-colorability, so it does not prove hardness of the fixed three-color target. Conversely, when a diameter-two instance already has a universal vertex, its 3-colorability reduces to checking that the remaining graph is bipartite.

The best general upper bound identified in the July 2026 source is subexponential: Dębski, Piecyk, and Rzążewski give time 2 raised to O(n^(1/3) log² n). Their algorithm combines branching, reductions to 2-SAT, and a structural observation proved probabilistically. The remaining gap is between this bound and polynomial time; the existence of a subexponential algorithm does not exclude NP-completeness.

Murakami’s July 2026 preprint proves polynomial-time list 3-coloring when the diameter-two graph contains no four-cycle even as a non-induced subgraph. Its discussion explicitly leaves the general diameter-two case open. The distinction matters: forbidding every four-cycle is stronger than forbidding only induced four-cycles, and neither condition is imposed here.

cards.title: Dynamic APSP with edge-linear updates
cards.formal: For every fixed positive integer c, do there exist a deterministic data structure and constants a,d >= 1 such that the following holds for all n >= 2 and $n\le m\le n^2$? Maintain a directed simple graph on a fixed set of n vertices, with at most m edges at every time and integer edge weights in {1,...,n^c}, under single-edge insertions, deletions, and weight changes. Return the exact current distance from any queried vertex s to any queried vertex t in $O(\log^a n)$ worst-case time. After $O(n^d)$ preprocessing, require $O(m\log^a n)$ amortized time per update and polynomial space. Constants may depend on c, but not on n, m, the initial graph, or the operation sequence.
cards.definitions: The capacity m is supplied in advance and bounds the maximum number of live edges throughout the sequence; it is not a count of all updates. Each ordered vertex pair has at most one edge and there are no self-loops. An insertion adds an absent edge, a deletion removes a present edge, and a weight change replaces the weight of one present edge by another permitted weight. A distance query returns the minimum sum of edge weights on a directed s-to-t path, zero for s=t, and a distinguished infinity value if no path exists. Only the distance is requested, not every path or the whole distance matrix. All answers must be exact for any interleaving of updates and queries. Use a word RAM with Theta(log n)-bit words, with a sufficiently large constant for the fixed weight exponent and polynomially bounded addresses; comparisons, arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, and random access cost one step. Amortization means that after preprocessing any U updates and Q queries together cost $O(U m\log^a n+Q\log^a n)$; the query bound must also hold for each query individually.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a data structure with these guarantees for every fixed polynomial weight bound, or prove that the quantified proposition is false. A conditional lower bound must state its assumption. A near-quadratic-in-n update bound only meets the target for dense graphs; a subpolynomial approximation ratio or a guarantee only for insertions does not meet the exact fully dynamic specification.
cards.why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.

importance.reason: A broad exact dynamic-graph frontier with a major sparse-versus-dense gap. It tests whether global metric information can be maintained at input-scale update cost while preserving fast queries.

progress.text: Demetrescu and Italiano give deterministic O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized updates and constant worst-case distance queries for general directed nonnegative-weight graphs.

Henzinger asks for fully dynamic APSP with edge-linear update cost and constant query cost, both allowing polylogarithmic factors. The fixed weight, edge-update, and amortization conventions here make that direction precise.
Mao’s revised paper gives a Monte Carlo algorithm with tilde-O(n^(5/2)) worst-case vertex-update time and near-quadratic space. This addresses a different update guarantee.

Kyng, Meierhans, and Zöcklein use sparsification for near-linear total processing of a bounded-length update sequence with polylogarithmic queries, but their returned distances have a subpolynomial approximation factor.

context_blocks.text: Recomputing distances from every source after each change is expensive, while postponing the work until a query can make a single query expensive. A dynamic distance oracle tries to divide this work so that both kinds of operation remain useful. The requested update budget is roughly the size of the current graph representation, even when that graph is sparse.

A single changed edge can alter distances for quadratically many vertex pairs. That observation does not by itself rule out a fast oracle: the representation may store those changes implicitly, and the interface only asks for one pair at a time. Proving a lower bound therefore requires more than counting changed entries in a materialized distance matrix.

The classical Demetrescu–Italiano algorithm achieves O(n^2 log^3 n) amortized update time and constant distance-query time for nonnegative weights. This is already close to the proposed bound when m is quadratic in n. The substantial gap is the sparse regime, where the desired amortized update cost can be nearly a factor n smaller.

Several nearby frontiers have different guarantees. Mao’s revised 2024 result targets worst-case vertex-update time and gives a randomized bound at the n^(5/2) scale. ESA 2025 sparsification gives extremely fast dynamic approximate distances, with a growing approximation factor. Neither result establishes the exact, edge-sensitive, amortized target on this card. Fixing those distinctions is necessary when assessing progress.

cards.title: Linear-space LZ77 random access
cards.formal: Given the greedy LZ77 parse with z phrases of a string $S[1..N]$ over an integer alphabet of size at most N, is there a deterministic word-RAM data structure using O(z) words in total that returns S[i] for any $1\le i\le N$ in worst-case O(log N) time? Words have $\Theta(\log N)$ bits. A phrase is a new literal or a longest prefix of the unparsed suffix having an occurrence starting earlier in S; overlapping copies are allowed. Space includes the stored parse and all query-support information. The uncompressed string is unavailable at query time.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform data structure meeting both bounds for every greedy LZ77 parse, or prove that no such structure exists in the stated model. Linear space measured by a larger grammar or an LZ-End parse does not meet the O(z) requirement.
cards.why: I include this because compression is most useful when a small representation remains usable for selective queries. This question asks whether an extra logarithmic storage cost is an inherent price of navigating repeated data or a consequence of converting to a more convenient representation.
cards.definitions: All asymptotic constants are universal. The model permits standard arithmetic, multiplication, shifts, bitwise operations, comparisons, and indirect addressing on a constant number of words. A copied phrase beginning at b and referring to a<b is decoded sequentially, so self-overlap is well-defined. Preprocessing may take polynomial time in N; the target concerns final storage and query time, not construction in compressed time. Use 1+log N at the smallest lengths.

progress.text: Ganardi, Jeż, and Lohrey show that a straight-line grammar can be balanced to logarithmic derivation depth with only constant-factor size growth. This settles the corresponding logarithmic-access target in terms of grammar size.
Gawrychowski explicitly asks for linear space in the Lempel–Ziv representation and logarithmic-time character access.

Boneh and Gawrychowski obtain deterministic O(z_end)-space random access in $O(1+\log^2(N/z_{\rm end}))$ time for LZ-End. Their introduction retains classical LZ77 random access as open and records $O(z\log(N/z))$-space solutions for it.

context_blocks.text: Lempel–Ziv compression replaces a repeated block by its earlier starting position and length. This can encode a long text with few phrases, but a position inside one copied phrase may lead to another copy, and then another. Random access asks for just one character without expanding the whole text.

The challenge is not that every deeply referenced string is hard. A long run of one repeated character can be accessed immediately once its simple structure is recognized. The target must work for arbitrary mixtures of copied material, where both the reference chains and the phrase lengths vary. Any shortcuts used to navigate those chains must fit in the compressed-space budget.

Converting the parse to a balanced grammar supplies a route to fast navigation, but the grammar can be larger than the original parse by a logarithmic factor. A space bound proportional to that grammar therefore need not be linear in z. Balancing a grammar already supplied as input is a different, solved representation problem.

The July 2026 LZ-End result is close in spirit: it obtains linear space and improved polylogarithmic access for a variant that restricts copy endpoints. Its parameter counts LZ-End phrases. Since the parsing rule and the number of phrases differ, those guarantees cannot be substituted directly for the classical LZ77 target.

cards.title: Linear-time LZ77 pattern matching
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm that, given a valid LZ77 representation of z phrases of a text T of length N and an explicit nonempty pattern P of length m, decides whether P occurs contiguously in T in O(z+m) worst-case time? Self-referencing copy phrases are allowed. Symbols are integers in $\{1,\ldots,(z+m)^c\}$ for a fixed constant c. Use a word RAM with word size $\Theta(\log(N+m+2))$, the operations specified below, and O(z+m) working words. The input is the compressed text and the explicit pattern; all preprocessing is included.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform algorithm with the stated bounds for every valid input, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The output is one yes/no answer. An algorithm linear in the uncompressed text length, or in a potentially larger grammar representation, does not attain this target.
cards.definitions: Each phrase is either one literal symbol or a pair (s,l) instructing the decoder to append l symbols copied sequentially from an earlier starting position s in the text. For a phrase beginning at p, require 1 <= s < p; the copied interval may overlap the phrase being produced. Phrase boundaries and references occupy O(1) words per phrase. No promise of a greedy parse is needed. The RAM has random access, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, and bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on a word at unit cost; arithmetic results are restricted to a word. There is no access to a separately stored decompressed text or precomputed index.
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether computation can follow the compressed input size rather than the size of the object it describes. cards.title: Grammar random access in O(g log g) bits
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic data structure that, for every binary straight-line program G with g rules generating a binary string T of length N, stores a representation in $O(g\log(g+2))$ bits and returns T[i] for any $1\le i\le N$ in $O(\log(N+2))$ worst-case time? Preprocessing must take time polynomial in g and is given G, not an expanded copy of T. The space bound includes every persistent index and any retained grammar. Use the word-RAM model below. The representation may replace G; it need only answer queries to T correctly.
cards.definitions: A binary straight-line program has ordered variables X_1,...,X_g, one rule per variable, and start variable X_g. A rule is X_j -> 0, X_j -> 1, or X_j -> X_a X_b with a,b < j. All variables must be reachable from the start variable. Expansion is unique and finite; g counts rules, not expanded occurrences. The input specifies rule types and indices in O(g log(g+2)) bits. Machine words have $\Theta(\log(N+g+2))$ bits; random access, comparisons, word addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division, Boolean operations, and shifts cost one step. Arithmetic results are restricted to a word. Stored bits may be packed; charge the final partially filled word as well. Queries may use O(log(N+2)) temporary words, initially empty and discarded afterward; this workspace contains no persistent advice. Every input-dependent table retained between queries counts toward the representation budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a uniform representation, preprocessing algorithm, and query algorithm satisfying all bounds for every valid G, or prove that no such data structure exists. Space linear in g machine words is insufficient when log N is asymptotically larger than log g. A scheme whose preprocessing first expands an exponentially longer T does not meet the polynomial-in-g preprocessing requirement.
cards.why: Random access is the simplest useful operation on a compressed string. cards.title: Matrix multiplication exponent
cards.formal: Fix the field of complex numbers. Let s(n) be the minimum number of arithmetic gates in a circuit that computes all entries of AB exactly for arbitrary n-by-n matrices A,B. Is it true that $\forall\varepsilon>0\;\exists C_\varepsilon>0\;\forall n\ge2:\ s(n)\le C_\varepsilon n^{2+\varepsilon}$? Equivalently, is $\omega=\inf\{\tau:s(n)=O(n^\tau)\}=2$?
cards.definitions: The inputs are 2n² independent complex variables a_ij,b_ij. The required n² output polynomials are c_ij=sum_{k=1}^n a_ik b_kj. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with binary addition, subtraction, and multiplication gates; any complex constants and unrestricted reuse of intermediate values are allowed. Size counts arithmetic gates, including operations involving constants. Input nodes, constant nodes, and output designations are not gates. No division, order comparisons, branching, approximation, or randomization is permitted. A different circuit may be chosen for every n: this is the standard nonuniform arithmetic-complexity formulation over C. The cost of encoding a complex number in bits is outside this model. The elementary lower bound s(n)>=n² for n>=2 follows because the n² distinct non-input output polynomials require distinct gates.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Matrix multiplication is a basic operation whose exponent enters many algorithms in linear algebra and graph theory. Determining whether its arithmetic cost can approach the quadratic scale would settle a central question about sharing computation among many related outputs.

importance.reason: One of the main questions in algebraic algorithms, governing a widely used primitive and many dependent complexity bounds. Both faster constructions and a superquadratic lower bound would have broad consequences.

context_blocks.text: The usual algorithm computes n² inner products of length n, spending cubic arithmetic work. That computation treats the outputs separately even though they share their input matrices. Strassen’s construction shows that this shared structure can save an asymptotic factor: seven block multiplications replace eight in a two-by-two block product, and recursive use gives exponent log₂7.

The question is whether one can keep reducing the extra exponent all the way to zero. Its quantifiers matter. An algorithm for each exponent 2+epsilon is enough, even when its constant depends badly on epsilon. Conversely, improving one decimal place in the current upper bound does not establish the conjecture. Fixing the field and counting exact scalar operations also separates this question from approximate numerical multiplication or hardware throughput.

Modern upper bounds encode multiplication in tensors and exploit savings across large tensor powers. A substantial part of their analysis can be expressed as an optimization over parameters. The August 2026 improvement expands that optimization and uses new search procedures to find better parameters; the paper then describes rational verification of the resulting inequalities. That is an arithmetic exponent result, not an empirical speed comparison.

There are also lower bounds on what specific tensor methods can achieve. For example, Alman’s universal-method barrier for Coppersmith–Winograd tensors prevents that route from reaching exponent two. It is not a lower bound on all arithmetic circuits for matrix multiplication. The distinction leaves room for different starting tensors or mathematical constructions.

cards.title: VP versus VNP
cards.formal: Over the field $\mathbb C$, do there exist constants C,k such that, for every integer n≥1, the polynomial $\operatorname{perm}_n(X)=\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n x_{i,\sigma(i)}$ can be computed by an arithmetic circuit with at most C(n+1)^k gates? Equivalently, is $\mathrm{VP}_{\mathbb C}=\mathrm{VNP}_{\mathbb C}$? The usual conjecture is that the answer is no.
cards.definitions: X has n² independent indeterminates and S_n is the set of permutations of {1,…,n}. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input nodes labeled by variables or arbitrary complex constants, binary +, −, × operation gates, and one output. Its size counts operation gates; intermediate results can feed any number of later gates. Division, comparisons, oracle gates, approximation, and limits of circuits are absent. The output must equal the permanent as a formal polynomial. Circuits may depend on n without a uniform construction algorithm; constants have unit arithmetic cost, with no bit-encoding restriction. VP consists of polynomial families with polynomially bounded numbers of variables and total degrees, computed by polynomial-size circuits. VNP consists of polynomial families f_n(x)=Σ_{y∈{0,1}^{p(n)}} g_n(x,y), for some polynomial p and some such polynomial-size, polynomial-degree circuit family g. The witness sum is over Boolean strings even though the coefficients lie in C.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct the stated circuit family, or prove that the minimum circuit size of the permanent is not bounded by any polynomial in n. A lower bound for every polynomial-size general circuit family suffices. Lower bounds only for formulas, monotone circuits, bounded-depth circuits, or determinantal representations do not by themselves settle this formulation.
cards.why: This is the central separation question for arithmetic computation. It tests whether summing exponentially many efficiently describable algebraic contributions inherently requires more computation than evaluating one polynomial-size circuit, and organizes lower-bound research across algebra, geometry, and pseudorandomness.

importance.reason: A foundational separation for general arithmetic circuits, with a complete concrete target in the permanent and consequences across algebraic complexity and explicit lower-bound constructions.

progress.text: Ryser’s inclusion-exclusion expression gives an exponential-size formula, for example O(n²2^n) arithmetic operations. This substantially improves direct enumeration of n! permutations but remains far above a polynomial bound.
Valiant establishes algebraic completeness of the permanent over fields of characteristic different from two. Over C this yields the equivalence between polynomial-size permanent circuits and VP=VNP.

Limaye, Srinivasan, and Tavenas prove superpolynomial lower bounds against arithmetic circuits of every constant depth in characteristic zero. Those circuits may have unbounded fan-in, with size accounting for their description; the fixed depth is an essential restriction. The result does not separate general VP and VNP.

Narayanan relates elusive polynomial maps to expansion of iterated sumsets and obtains improved superlinear bounds in certain sublogarithmic-depth regimes. An explicit elusive-curve construction has exponential degree; the paper explains that its parameters do not yet imply VP≠VNP.

context_blocks.text: The permanent sums one product for every perfect matching in a complete bipartite graph. Substituting a zero-one adjacency matrix counts perfect matchings. This card asks for an exact symbolic arithmetic computation valid on all complex matrices. The model permits cancellations and unrestricted reuse of intermediate results, so it captures substantially more than enumerating matchings.

The permanent and determinant have the same permutation products, but the determinant attaches a sign to each one. Determinants have polynomial-size division-free circuits despite their factorially many displayed terms. Thus counting the monomials in the permanent is not a circuit lower bound: the question is whether an equally effective algebraic compression exists for its unsigned sum.

Valiant makes this example universal. Every family in VNP reduces to a polynomially larger permanent by substitutions of variables and constants. A polynomial circuit for the permanent would therefore compress every efficient Boolean-witness sum in the definition of VNP. Conversely, separating these classes forces the permanent to escape polynomial circuit size.

Important partial results restrict how computations are organized. A formula cannot reuse an intermediate result; a constant-depth circuit permits only a fixed number of operation layers. Even proving that the permanent has no small determinant representation would rule out only that representation model. None of these restrictions is part of the circuit model in this card.

Recent lower bounds illustrate both the progress and the gap. Superpolynomial bounds are known at every fixed depth, and new work constructs polynomial maps that evade low-complexity parametrizations. The latter can yield stronger circuit lower bounds if its degree and dimension parameters improve sufficiently. The constructions currently cited do not give the required unrestricted superpolynomial bound.

cards.title: Cubic min-plus circuit lower bounds for shortest paths
cards.formal: For n >= 2, assign an arbitrary nonnegative real weight x_{ij} to every unordered edge {i,j} of the complete undirected graph on vertices 1,...,n. Define $f_n(x)=\min_{P:1\leadsto n}\sum_{e\in P}x_e$, where P ranges over simple paths. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input gates x_{ij} and optional constants 0 and infinity, binary gates min(a,b) or a+b, unrestricted reuse of gate outputs, and one designated output. Its topology depends on n but not on x, and it must compute f_n exactly for every permitted weight assignment. Let s(n) be the minimum number of binary gates in such a circuit. Is s(n)=Omega(n^3)? Equivalently, do there exist constants c>0 and n0 such that every such circuit has at least c n^3 gates for every n>=n0?
cards.definitions: A simple path visits no vertex twice. The two occurrences x_{ij} and x_{ji} denote the same input, because the graph is undirected. Infinity is an optional internal constant with min(a,infinity)=a and a+infinity=infinity; all input edge weights are finite and nonnegative. The circuit has no subtraction, tests with separate Boolean outputs, conditional routing, or input-dependent memory access. A min gate directly returns the smaller of its two numerical arguments. Input gates, wires, and reuse of an already computed value are free; binary arithmetic gates are counted. Circuits need not be generated uniformly by an efficient algorithm, so the proposed lower bound is nonuniform and imposes no depth restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified cubic lower bound, or refute it by proving its negation: for every c>0 and every n0 there is an n>=n0 with a correct circuit using fewer than c n^3 gates. An o(n^3)-size circuit family for all sufficiently large n would suffice for a negative answer. A lower bound for a more restricted circuit class, for all-pairs output, or for shortest paths allowing negative input weights does not establish this statement.
cards.why: This is a basic unconditional lower-bound question for dynamic programming. A resolution would clarify whether the standard cubic relaxation computation is intrinsically necessary even for one distance when computation is restricted to minimum and addition, and would illuminate why monotone lower-bound methods struggle with paths of varying lengths.

importance.reason: A central explicit lower-bound problem for tropical circuits, linking shortest paths, pure dynamic programming, and provenance computation. The gap concerns a basic polynomial-time task rather than a specialized graph family.

progress.text: Jukna gives the O(n^3) min-plus upper bound and explicitly asks for a cubic lower bound for the single-pair connectivity polynomial; his framework distinguishes nonnegative tropical evaluation from formal polynomial production.

A sample-complexity characterization should tell us how many labelled examples are necessary from the structure of the hypothesis class, rather than from a particular learning algorithm. The quantitative issue matters even after learnability is settled. Knowing that some finite sample size works does not distinguish a useful bound from an enormous one. cards.definitions: A concept class is a finite set of functions from a domain X to {0,1}. VC(C) is the largest size of a subset of X on which all binary labelings occur. LD(C) is the greatest depth of a complete binary tree labeled by domain points such that every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is realized by a concept. The function log-star counts base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. A learner may output a hypothesis outside C. Privacy requires $\Pr[A(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[A(S\prime)\in E]+1/(100m^2)$ whenever the two m-record samples differ by replacement of one record. Here X is finite, distributions on X are arbitrary probability vectors, and a learner is a probability kernel from length-m labeled samples to the finite set {0,1}^X of hypotheses. The sample size m is a positive integer chosen for C before the target and distribution. For every target h∈C and distribution D on X, with probability at least 9/10 over m independent draws x_i from D and learner randomness, the returned hypothesis has D-probability of disagreement with h at most 1/10. Privacy holds for all labeled samples, including unrealizable ones, and all subsets E of the hypothesis set. The same kernel and m work for all D,h. This finite-domain convention retains the finite-class target: points in an arbitrary domain with the same label vector (h(x))_{h∈C} can be identified, giving at most 2^|C| cells and preserving both dimensions. A learner on those cells lifts to the original domain. No running-time or computable-representation requirement is imposed.

cards.title: Conjunctive-query containment under bag semantics
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Does a Turing machine exist that halts on every pair of finite conjunctive queries q_1 and q_2 with the same output arity and decides whether $q_1(D)(a)\le q_2(D)(a)$ for every finite bag database D over their common relational signature and every output tuple a? A query $q(x)\!:\!-A_1,\ldots,A_m$ is evaluated by $q(D)(a)=\sum_{h:h(x)=a}\prod_{j=1}^{m}D(A_j[h])$, where h ranges over assignments of its variables to the finite database domain and D(A_j[h]) is the nonnegative integer multiplicity of the instantiated tuple. Both input relations and query answers retain multiplicities.
cards.definitions: A relational signature lists finitely many relation names and their arities. A finite bag database supplies a finite domain U and, for each relation symbol of arity r, a function U^r to the nonnegative integers. Zero means the tuple is absent. A query body is a finite list of positive relational atoms with variables or named constants as arguments; constants denote distinct fixed elements of U. Every variable, including every output variable, must occur in a body atom. Repeated occurrences of relation names, variables, or entire atoms are allowed and are interpreted by the displayed sum-product rule. Assignments fix constants. No disjunction, negation, inequality, comparison predicate, aggregation operator, or recursion is permitted. The output tuple lists the values of the head variables in order. Boolean queries have an empty head and return the multiplicity of the single empty tuple. The question is about deciding containment from the queries alone, with no database supplied and no size or multiplicity bound on databases.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a total algorithm deciding exactly this universal multiplicity inequality, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Enumerating counterexample databases only semidecides noncontainment. A procedure for set-valued databases, query equivalence, or a proper subclass of queries is insufficient; undecidability for unions, inequalities, or a modified numerical comparison is insufficient unless reduced to the stated plain-CQ problem.
cards.why: Bag semantics captures duplicate-sensitive query behavior, and containment is a basic correctness test for query optimization. Its unknown decidability marks a fundamental gap between simple positive query syntax and unbounded counting over finite structures. The problem also connects database theory with homomorphism inequalities and arithmetic decision problems.

importance.reason: A longstanding central decidability question for the most basic duplicate-sensitive query language. It has broad consequences for query rewriting and connects finite-model counting with undecidability boundaries.

context_blocks.text: Containment asks whether one query can ever produce more of some answer than another. Under set semantics only presence matters. Under bag semantics, a join multiplies available copies and projection adds contributions from different witnesses. The multiplicities can therefore change even when the two queries return exactly the same set of answers.

For a minimal example, let q(x) have body R(x), and let r(x) have body R(x),R(x). If R(a) has multiplicity m, then q returns m copies of a and r returns m^2. Their answer sets always coincide, but the reverse bag-containment r contained in q fails as soon as m=2. This demonstrates why duplicate-insensitive rewrites need a different correctness argument.

For one fixed finite database, both values can be computed by enumerating assignments. The challenge is the quantifier over every database of every size and every choice of multiplicities. Noncontainment has a finite witness that can eventually be found by exhaustive enumeration. A decision procedure also needs to halt when no witness exists; a counterexample search by itself does not solve that side.

The 2025 seminar still identifies this as a longstanding unresolved boundary. Recent work establishes decidability for a restricted left-hand query in which existential variables do not participate in joins, while related work proves undecidability after extending the query language or numerical comparison. These results make the precise boundary especially significant: small changes around the basic formulation have known answers, but do not settle two unrestricted plain conjunctive queries.

cards.title: Linear-round convergence over stable semirings
cards.area: Database theory and finite model theory
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that the following holds for every integer p>=0, every n>=1, every commutative p-stable semiring S, and every polynomial map F:S^n -> S^n with coefficients in S? Starting with x^(0)=(0,...,0), perform synchronous iteration x^(t+1)=F(x^(t)). There must exist an integer t<=C(p+1)n with x^(t+1)=x^(t). Here p-stability means $1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^p=1\oplus a\oplus\cdots\oplus a^{p+1}$ for every a in S. The constant C is independent of the semiring, coefficients, number of monomials, and polynomial degrees. cards.definitions: A commutative semiring has associative, commutative addition op-plus with identity 0 and associative, commutative multiplication op-times with identity 1. Multiplication distributes over addition, and 0 times a=0. No additive inverses are assumed. Powers use semiring multiplication and a^0=1. Every component of F is a finite sum of finite products of coefficients and variables; repeated variables and constant terms are allowed. S need not be finite. One round evaluates all components using only the previous vector, not partially updated coordinates. Equality means exact equality of semiring elements. The cost measure is the number of rounds, irrespective of the work needed to evaluate a component or represent an element. In a grounded Datalog program, coordinates represent individual derived facts and their values are annotations; using all n coordinates also includes any that remain zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal bound, or refute it by constructing systems whose first fixed-point time divided by (p+1)n is unbounded. A fixed example exceeding n rounds does not refute an unspecified constant C. A bound with a growing factor depending on degrees, coefficients, or n does not establish this target. A faster evaluation algorithm with a different update rule does not by itself bound the number of synchronous naive iterations.
cards.why: The problem asks whether local algebraic stability imposes a sharp global limit on recursive evaluation. A universal linear bound would explain why a broad class of annotated recursive computations needs only an output-scale number of rounds, while a separation would expose a fundamental cost of nonlinear interactions.

context_blocks.text: In ordinary Boolean Datalog, a derived fact switches from absent to present at most once. A nonstationary round must add a fact, so the number of possible facts bounds the number of rounds. Annotated recursion can improve the value attached to an already known fact many times. Counting how many coordinates exist therefore ceases to give an immediate termination bound.

The stability assumption controls repeated use of a single semiring element. It says that a sufficiently long truncated geometric sum absorbs the next power. The question asks whether a system of n interacting recurrences can multiply the resulting delay by only O(n), even when the equations are nonlinear. This is a structural claim about composition of recursive dependencies, not a bound on the time taken by one database join.

The examined Im–Moseley–Ngo–Pruhs preprint proves a polynomial convergence bound, with explicit dependence on sigma, the number of distinct coefficients referenced, and lambda, the maximum number of multiplicands. Its bound is O(sigma p n^2 (n^2 log(lambda+1)+log(sigma+1))) for positive p; the 0-stable case has a separate linear bound. Suppressing sigma and lambda would conceal part of the remaining challenge.

The 2025 seminar asks for O((p+1)n), matching the order of its stated lower bound. A newer paper titled Optimal Convergence of Iterative Methods for Datalogo is now listed by its authors. The inspected listings supply no theorem or accessible manuscript for that entry. cards.formal: For every finite input schema and every generic query q expressible by a safe, constant-free stratified Datalog program with disequality, suppose that q is preserved under induced extensions of finite database instances. cards.definitions: Fix an infinite set D of data values. An input schema is a finite set of relation names with specified finite arities. A database instance I is a finite set of facts R(a₁,…,aᵣ), with aᵢ∈D. Its active domain adom(I) is the set of values occurring in those facts. J is an induced extension of I when adom(I)⊆adom(J) and, for every input relation R of arity r, Rᴵ=Rᴶ∩adom(I)ʳ. Thus all relations on old tuples are unchanged; every new fact of positive arity contains at least one new value. Nullary facts must remain unchanged. A query q of arity k maps I to a finite set of k-tuples, and is generic if permuting D commutes with q. For k=0, the empty tuple represents true. Membership in E means q(I)⊆q(J) for every such pair I,J. A program has finitely many rules H(ȳ)←A₁,…,Aᵤ,¬B₁,…,¬Bᵥ,z₁≠w₁,…,zₛ≠wₛ. Atoms use relation names and variables, with no constants, function symbols or value invention. Every variable in the head, a negative atom or a disequality must also occur in a positive body atom. Input relations are extensional and never defined by a rule; derived relations are intensional. A stratification assigns levels to intensional relations so that positive dependencies have no higher level than the head and negative dependencies have strictly lower level. Evaluate levels in order, starting new derived relations empty and repeatedly adding every head whose instantiated body holds until no further fact is added; lower levels and input facts stay fixed. The distinguished output relation defines q. A semi-positive program permits negative atoms only on input relations. Equality can be represented by repeated variables, and disequality is actual inequality of data values. Programs may introduce finitely many auxiliary intensional relations of arbitrary finite arity. The requested equivalence is equality of outputs on every finite input instance, with no built-in order or additional input relations.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every query satisfying the stated stratified definability and extension-preservation conditions has a semi-positive definition, or exhibit a stratified extension-preserved query and prove that no semi-positive program with disequality defines it. Failure of one proposed rewrite is insufficient. The claim concerns existence of equivalent definitions; it imposes neither an effective recognition algorithm for E nor a bound on rewrite size.
